mem.t: Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

lessons.title: You Are the Salt
lessons.theme: Not seasoning for show, but keeping things from going bad

v: “You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavour, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men.
Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”

lessons.still: Before you leave home, put a hand on your chest and be still for thirty seconds. Say to the Lord: “Lord, if there is rot in the places I walk into today, make me that pinch of salt—not by my loud voice, but by your life in me.”
teach: On a hillside Jesus looked at fishermen, farmers and ordinary villagers and said, “You are the salt of the earth.” Notice that he did not say, “Try hard to become salt.” He said, “You are.” This is a declaration of identity, not a performance target. In a world without fridges, salt's main job was to stop decay: a fish rubbed with salt could travel for days without rotting. Salt works quietly. It does not draw attention, yet it decides whether things spoil. And Jesus warns that salt which has lost its flavour is “good for nothing.” Its value lies in staying different.

In today's office, salt is like a fuse in the fuse box. When the current surges out of control, the fuse would rather burn out than let the whole building catch fire. A screenshot of the boss forwarded round the group chat, gossip embroidered at the coffee machine, the little expense-claim fiddle that “everyone does”—corruption usually travels as a chain reaction, passed from one person to the next. The Christian is the one with whom it stops: not forwarding, not joining in, not taking part, and yet not standing above others in judgement. One small fuse protects the whole system.

Jesus also said, “Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another” (Mark 9:50). Salt does not only preserve outwardly; it brings peace inwardly. This is the 321 pattern from the inside out: life first, then relationships, then ministry. If our hearts are self-centred—wanting to prove we are purer than others—our saltiness turns into a bitter sting. True saltiness is the self-emptied life of Christ living in me: refusing corruption while embracing people, holding principles without hurting people for the sake of a task.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your mindset and your life changes—from “I'm just a junior employee; what can I change?” to “I am the salt of the earth.” That is God's view, not man's. Salt does not win by quantity but by keeping its nature, and my nature is Christ in me.
lessons.scene: Qianyu is in her second year as an audit associate at an accounting firm. On Friday night someone in her intake's group chat posts a photo of their manager dining with a client, with a suggestive joke. A dozen people reply with laughing stickers. Then someone tags her: “Qianyu, you're the good girl—what do you think?” Her thumb hovers over the screen.
q: Who is God? — When Jesus says, “You are the salt of the earth,” what does it show you about how he sees ordinary followers?
Who am I? — In your workplace, what “chain reaction of decay” is passing through your hands right now?
How shall I respond? — If you were Qianyu, how would you reply without joining in, and without making your colleagues feel judged?
lessons.jesus: A man with leprosy came to Jesus, and everyone else kept their distance, but Jesus “stretched out his hand and touched him” (Matthew 8:3). By normal rules, touching a leper made you unclean. With Jesus, cleanness flowed into uncleanness, not the other way round. He is the true salt: entering the most corrupted places and bringing healing there.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for calling me the salt of the earth. I confess that I often fear being left out, so I laugh along, forward along, complain along. Keep my saltiness from fading. In the group chat, in meetings, on my expense forms, make me the one with whom it stops, and let my words carry kindness rather than judgement. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Today, don't forward or add to gossip or grumbling
Silently pray once for a colleague people talk about
Check one form you handled and make sure it's fully honest
lessons.noon: “You are the salt of the earth” — Lord, right now help me keep my flavour in small things and not drift with the crowd.

lessons.title: A Lamp on the Stand
lessons.theme: Light is not meant to hide but to shine for everyone in the house

v: You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”

lessons.still: Before you switch on your computer, pause for thirty seconds. Close your eyes and picture Jesus placing a lit lamp in your hands. Tell him: “Lord, you are the light of the world. Today I won't switch the lamp off, and I won't show it off; I only want your light to shine through me.”
teach: On the hills of Galilee, after dark, you could often see a town on a far hilltop glittering with lamps, impossible to hide. Jesus used that picture: “A city located on a hill can't be hidden.” Then he described something every household knew: no one lights a lamp and covers it with a measuring basket. You put it on a stand, “and it shines to all who are in the house.” Light by nature is meant to be seen and to light up others. Hiding the lamp is not humility; it is waste.

Many Christians have set their faith at work to “private account”—visible only to church friends, hidden from colleagues. We fear labels; we fear being accused of preaching. So the lamp goes under the basket. But light doesn't need a loudspeaker; it only needs to be there. A desk lamp in the right place doesn't shout at anyone, and the whole room simply grows brighter. Answering honestly when asked about your weekend, owning a mistake openly, quietly giving thanks before lunch—each is a small step from “private” back to “public.”

We can shine only because Jesus first said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). We are not power stations; we are lamps. The source is him, not our charm. This removes two kinds of self-centredness: hiding for fear of embarrassment, and performing to be noticed. 321 says the focus is on Jesus, not on myself. With my eyes on him, I need neither hide nor perform. I simply follow.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example—he is the light of the world, and following him I have light. Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself: no need to scheme how to “package” your faith; simply follow each day, and the light will sit on its stand.
lessons.scene: Bojun has just transferred to a new software team. At the first weekly meeting the manager asks everyone for a one-minute introduction, “and tell us what you do at weekends.” The colleagues before him mention football, box sets, ferrying the kids around. He is next—and every weekend he leads a small group of young teenagers at church.
q: Who is God? — Jesus says, “I am the light of the world.” How does this change your understanding of where your own light comes from?
Who am I? — Is your faith at work more like a “private account” or a “public account”? Why?
How shall I respond? — If you were Bojun, how would you introduce yourself in one natural, unawkward minute?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not hide away in Nazareth, nor did he build a stage in Jerusalem to perform. He walked among fishing boats, tax booths, wells and sickbeds, and his light came into one home after another. In the end he was lifted high on a cross outside the city—the darkest hour, which became the lampstand that lights the whole world.
lessons.pray: Jesus, light of the world, I confess I often hide my faith, afraid of labels and laughter; and sometimes I want people to see how good I am. Cleanse me of both. Today, in introductions, in meetings, at the lunch table, let me naturally live as one who follows you, so that my colleagues see not me but your light. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: If asked about your weekend, mention church naturally
Give thanks quietly before lunch—no hiding, no show
When you make a mistake, own it straight away
lessons.noon: “He who follows me will not walk in the darkness” — Lord, right now I don't shine by myself; I simply follow you.

lessons.title: What More Do You Do?
lessons.theme: The Christian difference is not the packaging but the recipe of love

v: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy.’
But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,
that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.
For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
If you only greet your friends, what more do you do than others? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?
Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Dividing his garments amongst them, they cast lots.

lessons.still: Once you're on the bus or train, take thirty seconds to think: who is the person you'd most like to avoid today? Say their name in your heart and tell the Lord: “Lord, you make your sun rise on the evil and the good. Today let your love shine through me onto them too.”
teach: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus asked two sharp questions: “If you love those who love you, what reward do you have?” and “If you only greet your friends, what more do you do than others?” In those days tax collectors were seen as greedy collaborators, yet Jesus said even they understood give-and-take. He was not asking for slightly better manners but for an entirely different love: “love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you.” This love comes from the Father, for “he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good.”

In business everyone talks about “differentiation.” If two bubble-tea shops have the same menu, the same prices and the same cups, customers can't tell them apart. Many Christians at work are a “commodity product”: kind to those who are kind to me, cold to those who poach my sales—just like any other colleague. The difference Jesus means is not a more spiritual-looking cup sleeve but an entirely different recipe: when others retaliate, we bless; when others count the return, we give freely. That is what saltiness tastes like.

This love is not squeezed out through gritted teeth. For the self-centred, love is a transaction: what you give me, I give back. The self-emptied life is Christ living in me, his love flowing through me. 321 says pride provokes pride and both lose; humility draws out humility and both win. When we stop rushing to get justice for ourselves and hand justice to God, we make room for his love to work. That is the Christian's real “more.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Don't hurt people for the sake of targets, and don't wreck a relationship over one lost customer. Shifting from the human view (an eye for an eye) to God's view (sun on the evil and the good)—that is saltiness.
lessons.scene: Fengying has sold vegetables at a Penang morning market for fifteen years. The new stall next door keeps undercutting her and tells regulars her produce isn't fresh. This morning their chiller has broken down, and crates of leafy greens are about to wilt in the heat. The owner comes over, eyes red: “Could I borrow your socket and a bit of ice?”
q: Who is God? — “He makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good.” What does this show you about the Father's heart?
Who am I? — At work, is your love more like “give-and-take” or “giving freely”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Fengying, how would you respond to the neighbour who has spoken against you?
lessons.jesus: Nails pierced his hands and feet; soldiers gambled for his clothes at his feet. Yet Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He did not love only those who loved him; at his enemies' cruellest moment he prayed for them. We can love the hard-to-love today because we ourselves were enemies who have been forgiven.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for making your sun rise on the good and the evil—and on me, who doesn't deserve it. I confess my love is often calculated: warm to those who are good to me, cold to those who hurt me. Put the heart Jesus had on the cross within me. Today let me pray for the colleague who took my credit and spoke badly of me, and help me reach out when he is in need. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray once, by name, for a difficult colleague
Greet someone who has been cold to you
Do a small favour for someone who can't repay you
lessons.noon: “love your enemies, bless those who curse you” — Lord, right now let me pray for that person.

lessons.title: The Exhibit, Not the Spotlight
lessons.theme: Good works aim to lead people to glorify the Father

v: Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
Then this Daniel was distinguished above the presidents and the local governors, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.

Then the presidents and the local governors sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.
Then these men said, “We won’t find any occasion against this Daniel, unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God.”

lessons.still: Before you walk into the office, stop at the door for thirty seconds. Pray quietly: “Father, in every good thing I do today, may people see not my name but your glory.” Then push the door open.
teach: Daniel served as an official in a foreign court. He had “an excellent spirit,” and his rivals “could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful.” Jealous colleagues combed through his record and found nothing, until they said, “We won't find any occasion against this Daniel, unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God.” What an appraisal: the only thing his enemies could attack was his faith. His good work was not about promotion but faithfulness to God—and in the end King Darius saw the living God behind Daniel.

Jesus said, “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” Good works are like the spotlight in a museum display case. Good lighting design makes visitors marvel at the exhibit, not stare at the ceiling. If all people remember is “what a bright lamp,” the lighting has failed. Meeting deadlines, being honest with clients, being fair to your team—these are the lamp. Where is it pointing? At God.

There is a subtle balance here. In the same sermon Jesus warns against doing good “before men, to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1). The difference is motive: do I want them to see me, or to see God? Self-centred good works end in my reputation; self-emptied good works end in the Father's glory. 321 says, let Jesus receive all the glory. When praised, we need neither push it away with false modesty nor pocket all of it; we can honestly point the light back to its source.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory—good works are the lamp; the glory belongs to God. Humility is returning to my proper place: I am the lamp, not the exhibit. Let people be people, and let God be God.
lessons.scene: Tianyou works at the counter of a district household registration office. An elderly man has written to the district head, thanking him by name for patiently helping him finish paperwork he'd failed at on three trips. At the morning briefing the section chief reads the letter aloud, then asks, “Tianyou, how do you manage to be so patient every day?” Every head turns towards him.
q: Who is God? — From Daniel's story, what do you see about how God uses someone who works faithfully?
Who am I? — When you're praised, how do you usually react? Keep the credit, push it away, or point to God?
How shall I respond? — If you were Tianyou, how would you answer the chief so the light points to God without sounding preachy?
lessons.jesus: Jesus performed many miracles yet often told people not to spread the news. He said, “I don't seek my own glory” (John 8:50). On the eve of his betrayal he prayed to the Father, “I glorified you on the earth” (John 17:4). His finest works were all spotlights turned towards the Father—and on Easter morning the Father himself glorified his Son.
lessons.pray: Father in heaven, thank you for opportunities to do good at work. I confess I long to be seen and affirmed, and sometimes I fake modesty. Make me faithful like Daniel, so people find no fault in me but can see your hand. If someone praises me today, let me thank them sincerely and honestly give the glory to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Finish one task so well no fault can be found
When praised, thank them, and give God the glory inwardly
Do one favour secretly, telling no one
lessons.noon: “glorify your Father who is in heaven” — Lord, right now let everything I do be for your glory.

lessons.title: What Light Does My Office Need?
lessons.theme: Lighting my corner of work with goodness, righteousness and truth

v: For you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light,
for the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth,
proving what is well pleasing to the Lord.
Have no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness, but rather even reprove them.
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.

lessons.still: When you sit down, spend thirty seconds looking around: your desk, your colleagues, the view from the window. Say in your heart: “Lord, this is where you have sent me. Show me which kind of light this place needs most.”
teach: Paul reminded the Ephesians, “You were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.” Then he described what light looks like: “the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth.” Light is not a vague spiritual feeling but visible fruit. Paul adds that we are to be “proving what is well pleasing to the Lord”—children of light don't shine blindly; they shine with discernment.

Lighting designers know that different spaces need different light. An operating theatre needs bright, shadowless light; a warehouse needs even, durable light; a café needs warm, soft light. Your office is the same. A department that passes the buck most needs the light of truth—someone willing to say, “That was my mistake.” A cold team most needs the light of goodness—someone who remembers the new starter's name. A place where favour decides everything most needs the light of righteousness—someone who won't play favourites. First discern, then shine.

This week we have begun learning to be ambassadors at work through salt and light. The source of light is not us but the Lord whose “light shines in the darkness” (John 1:5). 321 reminds us: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When my life is lit by him, I can light up those connected to me, and finally help build God's order at work. Here is the 920 practice: every colleague is one of my “2”, the people in my life; before them I live the self-emptied “0”, so that goodness, righteousness and truth become the visible “9”, the fruit of the Spirit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Building God's order begins with a single lamp. From the inside out: let the light reach my mindset and my life first, then my daily living and relationships, and finally become ministry that changes my department.
lessons.scene: Shu Fen is an admin manager at a logistics firm in Singapore. At the monthly meeting the new manager asks everyone to write, anonymously, “the one thing our team most needs to improve.” She thinks of padded overtime claims, new starters left to fend for themselves, and everyone blaming each other for mistakes—all true. Pen in hand, she can't decide which to write, or whether she's willing to change first herself.
q: Who is God? — “The light shines in the darkness.” What does this show you about how Jesus faces the world's darkness?
Who am I? — Goodness, righteousness, truth: which light do you yourself most often lack?
How shall I respond? — If you were Shu Fen, which would you write? And how would you begin with yourself?
lessons.jesus: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn't overcome it” (John 1:5). Jesus did not wait for the world to be ready. He came into a world that did not welcome him—rejected, misunderstood—yet he kept shining, all the way to the cross and the empty tomb. Darkness has never overcome the light, so we need not wait for our office to improve before we shine.
lessons.pray: Lord of light, thank you for bringing me out of darkness into your wonderful light. Help me discern which light my office needs most: truth, goodness or righteousness. And shine on me first, so that I am willing to be first to admit fault, first to care, first to be fair. Today, from my own desk, let your light shine out. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the one light your office needs most
Live out that light yourself once today
Learn a new colleague's name and greet them
lessons.noon: “Walk as children of light” — Lord, right now let me shine your light in this corner.

mem.t: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear.

lessons.title: The Crash Cart, Always Stocked
lessons.theme: Honour Christ as holy in your heart, and hope will find its answer

v: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,
having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.

lessons.still: Before you head out, stand still for thirty seconds and say softly: “Lord Christ, today be holy and great in my heart. If anyone asks why I still have hope, put the words in my mouth and gentleness in my heart.”
teach: Peter was writing to scattered believers who were often misunderstood and even slandered. He did not send them out to debate in the streets. He said, “Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear.” The order matters: first the heart, then the mouth; first honouring the Lord, then answering people. And notice: “everyone who asks.” Witness is often not something we force on others; it is others seeing a hope in us and being unable not to ask.

Every hospital ward has a crash cart. Most days nobody notices it, but the nurses check it every shift: are the drugs in date, is the defibrillator charged? When a patient suddenly collapses, there's no time to run to the stores. “Always be ready” is like that cart: not used every day, but when it is needed, it must be full, working and to hand. Ready with what? A heart that honours the Lord as holy, a real story of what he has done, and a few simple, clear words.

Peter adds, “having a good conscience.” Our answers carry weight not because we are eloquent but because our lives match our words. This is “live it first, then say it”: life first, then ministry. If self-centredness fills the heart, our answers turn into arguments, lectures or showing off; if the Lord is honoured in our hearts, our answers carry gentleness and reverence. We are not trying to win a debate but to let people see the Lord who gives us hope.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting Jesus be King begins with honouring Christ as holy in your heart. The focus is on Jesus, not on your eloquence. Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself—prepare your heart, and the Spirit will give you fitting words in the moment.
lessons.scene: Jun'an is a site supervisor for a construction firm in Kuala Lumpur. Rumours say the company will cut a third of its staff, and at lunch in the site cabin everyone looks grim. The oldest foreman suddenly turns to him: “Jun'an, your wife's just had your second baby—how can you still eat and sleep? What are you leaning on?” Everyone goes quiet, waiting for his answer.
q: Who is God? — “Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts.” What kind of Lord is he, that he deserves such honour?
Who am I? — If someone asked you today about the reason for your hope, would your “crash cart” be full or empty?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jun'an, how would you answer the foreman in a minute or two, gently and honestly?
lessons.jesus: Jesus stood before Pilate with his life in the governor's hands. He neither begged nor raged, but calmly said, “For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth” (John 18:37). His hope was not in a Roman governor's hands but in the Father's. That calm is the ground on which we answer everyone.
lessons.pray: Lord Christ, today be holy and great in my heart, greater than my job, my pay and my prospects. When colleagues ask why I still have hope, keep me from panic and from preaching; let me answer with gentleness and reverence. Cleanse my conscience too, so that my life is worthy of what I say. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write three sentences on “why I have hope”
Pause once today to honour the Lord in your heart
Notice an anxious colleague and check in with them
lessons.noon: “sanctify the Lord God in your hearts” — Lord, right now you are great in my heart; I need not panic.

lessons.title: Heaven's Expat on Assignment
lessons.theme: When misunderstood, good conduct is the best reply

v: Beloved, I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims to abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul,
having good behaviour amongst the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation.
When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.

lessons.still: Before you swipe into work, take three deep breaths. Tell the Lord: “Lord, I am a foreigner here, your representative. If anyone misunderstands or mocks me today, help me, like Jesus, not to curse back, but to entrust myself to you.”
teach: Peter calls believers “foreigners and pilgrims.” In the Roman Empire they were often seen as odd: refusing idols looked irreverent; staying away from wild parties looked antisocial. Peter did not tell them to issue statements in their defence. He said, “having good behaviour amongst the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation.” Time speaks, and so do good works.

Staff posted abroad by multinational firms know that everything they do represents not just themselves but head office. Local colleagues may never read the company's vision statement, but they will judge what kind of firm it is by how the expat manager treats the cleaners and handles complaints. Christians at work are heaven's expats on assignment. Colleagues may never read the Bible, but they read us every day. How we respond to mockery often introduces our “head office” more clearly than any sermon.

Peter also urges us “to abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul.” When we are misunderstood, the strongest craving is often to win back our dignity and prove ourselves right—self-centredness struggling to take the throne. 321 says humility is the key to revival, and humility draws out humility. When we stop rushing to defend ourselves and keep responding with good conduct, we hand judgement back to God: let people be people, and let God be God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift perspective—from the temporary (today's sting of being misread) to the eternal (God glorified in the day of visitation). Don't hurt people to settle a score; answering with good conduct is how we let Jesus be King.
lessons.scene: Philip is a night-shift supervisor at a dairy factory in New Zealand. His colleague Wayne calls him “Saint Philip,” joking about the fact that he doesn't drink or swear. Tonight Wayne has set the pasteurisation temperature wrong; a whole batch may have to be scrapped, and he's gone white. The quality report must go in before dawn, and Philip's name is on the signature line.
q: Who is God? — “Glorify God in the day of visitation.” What does this show you about how God sees time and justice?
Who am I? — When you are misunderstood or mocked, what is the strongest craving in your heart?
How shall I respond? — If you were Philip, how would you handle the report honestly, and how would you treat Wayne?
lessons.jesus: “When he was cursed, he didn't curse back. When he suffered, he didn't threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). Jesus was mocked and falsely accused, yet he spoke not one word of revenge. That was not weakness; he placed his case in the Father's hands. The Roman centurion at the cross glorified God after watching him die that way.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, when you were cursed you didn't curse back; when you suffered you didn't threaten. Yet I want to explain myself the moment I'm misread, and hit back the moment I'm mocked. Remind me that I am a foreigner here and your representative. Today make me honest in my report, kind to my colleagues, and trusting you when I'm misunderstood. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When teased today, smile instead of hitting back
Do a favour for a colleague who has mocked you
Write reports truthfully—no blame-shifting, no exaggeration
lessons.noon: “having good behaviour amongst the nations” — Lord, right now let my conduct speak for you.

lessons.title: One Sentence from a Servant Girl
lessons.theme: A sincere referral can change someone's whole life

v: Now Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the LORD had given victory to Syria; he was also a mighty man of valour, but he was a leper.
The Syrians had gone out in bands, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little girl, and she waited on Naaman’s wife.
She said to her mistress, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him of his leprosy.”
Someone went in and told his lord, saying, “The girl who is from the land of Israel said this.”
Then went he down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.

He returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and came, and stood before him; and he said, “See now, I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel. Now therefore, please take a gift from your servant.”

lessons.still: Before you go out, be still for thirty seconds and pray for the person you will serve most today: “Lord, you see their trouble. If there is an opening today, give me one sentence that points to you, the God who heals.”
teach: Naaman was commander of the Syrian army, “a great man with his master, and honourable,” “a mighty man of valour”—and then Scripture adds, “but he was a leper.” In his household was a little girl taken captive from Israel, who waited on Naaman's wife. She had no name, no status; she was a casualty of war. We can imagine she might have kept a resentful silence. Instead she said, “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Then he would heal him of his leprosy.” That one sentence reached the king and changed a general's life.

In a hospital, what changes a patient's outcome is sometimes not the consultant who operates but the referral letter. The local GP says, “With these symptoms, you need to see a specialist at the hospital.” The girl made a referral: she couldn't heal leprosy, but she knew who could. Witness at work is like that. You don't need to be a theologian or solve all your colleague's problems. You only need to know who can, and at the right moment say that one sincere sentence.

The most moving thing about this girl is her goodwill towards the household that had carried her off. That is the self-emptied life—denying self means living for Jesus and for others, not for myself. Naaman dipped seven times in the Jordan, his flesh was restored, and he said, “See now, I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel.” One sentence of witness led one man to know God. Our one sentence may be a referral letter God has already prepared.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-denial—living for Jesus and for others, not for myself. In adversity the girl was not bound by bitterness; she let God be King through her. When the self-emptied life comes first, that one sentence carries weight.
lessons.scene: Youzhen has worked as a home cleaner in Taichung for five years and cleans for a lawyer's wife every Tuesday. Today, as she arrives, the woman is on the sofa with red eyes. Her husband's scan has shown a shadow on his lung; he has a biopsy next week, and she hasn't slept. Youzhen is still holding the mop. There is a sentence in her heart, but she doesn't know whether to say it.
q: Who is God? — From Naaman's healing, what do you see about God's heart for “outsiders”?
Who am I? — In your work, do you also feel too small to speak for God?
How shall I respond? — If you were Youzhen, what would your one sentence be, and how would you say it gently?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). The King of kings came not as a general but as a servant. He did not issue commands from a palace; he spoke words of life in people's homes, at sickbeds and around dinner tables. The nameless servant girl seems to foreshadow this servant King.
lessons.pray: Lord, I often feel like a nobody whose words carry no weight. Thank you for using a nameless servant girl. As I serve people, give me eyes to see their trouble, a heart free of bitterness, and one sentence that points to you. If someone needs it today, give me courage to ask, “May I pray for you?” In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Notice someone who is going through a hard time
Prepare one sentence: “May I pray for you?”
Say it once today, or pray for them silently
lessons.noon: “I wish that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria” — Lord, right now make me a sentence that points to you.

lessons.title: Before-and-After Photos
lessons.theme: Before, meeting Jesus, now—and Jesus is the main character

v: I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he counted me faithful, appointing me to service,
although I used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. However, I obtained mercy because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.
He therefore answered, “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.”

lessons.still: Once you're seated on your commute, close your eyes for thirty seconds and recall the moment you first truly met Jesus. Tell him: “Lord, thank you for finding me that day. If anyone asks about the change in me today, let everything I say be about you.”
teach: Writing to Timothy, Paul tells his story in a few verses. Before: “I used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent.” Meeting: “I obtained mercy,” because “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.” Now: grace “abounded exceedingly with faith and love,” and the Lord was “appointing me to service.” He even calls himself the “chief” of sinners, because in him Jesus would “display all his patience” as an example for others. Paul's testimony does not boast about himself; it boasts about the Lord's patience.

Renovation firms love to put before-and-after photos in their portfolios: on one side a damp, leaking old flat, on the other a bright, warm new home. But a savvy client asks, “Who did the work in between?” A life testimony is the same. Many testimonies only say “how bad it was” or “how good it is now,” and never make clear the builder in the middle. A good three-minute testimony gives roughly a third to before, a third to meeting Jesus, a third to now—and Jesus, who did the work, runs through all of it.

The man born blind in John 9, under the Pharisees' interrogation, could offer no theology, but he said, “One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.” That is the power of testimony: honest, concrete, impossible to refute. Change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your daily living changes. Your “before, meeting, now” is a true record of that fivefold change from the inside out. It need not be dramatic; it only needs to be true.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory—the main character of my testimony is not my change but the Lord who changed me. The fivefold change—mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry—is the skeleton of my story.
lessons.scene: Deborah is a paralegal at a Singapore law firm. Over lunch her long-time colleague Mei Ling suddenly says, “You used to get so wound up—one little thing and you couldn't sleep. The last two years you've been different. What happened?” Deborah's heart leaps, but she worries about saying too much and scaring her off. Only twenty minutes of lunch are left.
q: Who is God? — Paul says the Lord displayed “all his patience” in him. What patience of the Lord do you see in your own life?
Who am I? — What are your “before, meeting, now”? Which part is hardest for you to put into words?
How shall I respond? — If you were Deborah, how would you tell your change in three minutes, with Jesus as the main character?
lessons.jesus: In the middle of every true testimony stands the same Jesus. He stopped Saul, the persecutor of the church, on the Damascus road; he put mud on the blind man's eyes; and at some turning in your life he called your name. The heart of testimony is never “I got better,” but “he came, and he saved me, a sinner.”
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for displaying all your patience in me. You know who I used to be, and I remember how you found me. Help me put this story together clearly—no exaggerating, no hiding—so that those who hear see not how good I am but how good you are. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write one sentence: “Before, I was…”
Write one sentence: “How I met Jesus…”
Write one sentence: “Now, I am…”
lessons.noon: “One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.” — Lord, right now I remember what you have done for me.

lessons.title: Go Home and Tell Them
lessons.theme: Write down what the Lord has done for me, ready to tell it

v: As he was entering into the boat, he who had been possessed by demons begged him that he might be with him.
He didn’t allow him, but said to him, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you.”
He went his way, and began to proclaim in Decapolis how Jesus had done great things for him, and everyone marvelled.
Come and hear, all you who fear God. I will declare what he has done for my soul.

lessons.still: Once you're on your commute, open the notes app on your phone, but don't write yet. Be still for thirty seconds and tell the Lord: “Lord, you have done great things for me. Help me write them down, and prepare me to tell them.”
teach: The man who had been possessed by demons and lived among the tombs, once set free by Jesus, “begged him that he might be with him.” It was a natural desire: who wouldn't want to stay beside the Saviour? But Jesus didn't allow it. He said, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you.” He had no training and had never written a sermon, but he went and “began to proclaim in Decapolis how Jesus had done great things for him, and everyone marvelled.”

Before founders meet investors, they always prepare a one-page summary: the problem, the solution, the results. Not because the business is that simple, but because the investor only has a few minutes. A three-minute testimony is the one-pager of your life. Today, write it down: around four to five hundred words, free of church jargon, as if chatting with a colleague who has never been to church. Read it aloud and time it. Cut the extra adjectives; keep the concrete details.

The psalmist says, “Come and hear, all you who fear God. I will declare what he has done for my soul” (Psalm 66:16). Writing a testimony is itself worship, and it practises “review and correction” from the eight steps: looking back at how God changed my mindset, life and daily living. Once it's written, the next steps are “practice and repetition”—tell it first to a spiritual companion, then get ready to tell a colleague. The multiplication of 235 begins with one testimony spoken aloud.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The last of the eight steps is multiplication. Jesus sent the man home so that he would pass on what he had received. Write it for yourself first, tell it to a spiritual companion next, then share it with your “2”, the people God has put in your life.
lessons.scene: Zhigang is production manager at an electronics factory in Shenzhen. Before the year-end dinner the boss tells every manager to take three minutes on stage to share “my biggest change this year.” His biggest change: after a major quality incident he came to faith and stopped screaming at his staff. He's on stage tonight, and his page is still blank.
q: Who is God? — Jesus didn't let the man follow him but sent him home. What does this show you about Jesus' purpose?
Who am I? — From whom do you most often hide “what the Lord has done for me”? Why?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zhigang, how would you share your change in three minutes, honestly and appropriately?
lessons.jesus: Jesus refused the man's request, not because he didn't love him, but because he also loved his family and the whole Decapolis. He sent him home, just as the Father sent the Son into the world. Jesus himself is the faithful witness sent by the Father; our testimony continues his sending.
lessons.pray: Lord, you have done great things for me, and I remember how you had mercy on me. Help me today to write it down in simple, sincere words, without exaggerating or hiding. Prepare a spiritual companion to hear me practise, and prepare a colleague's heart to listen when the time is right. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write the first draft of your three-minute testimony
Read it aloud, time it, trim it under three minutes
Ask a spiritual companion to hear you tell it
lessons.noon: “tell them what great things the Lord has done for you” — Lord, right now I remember your grace and get ready to tell it.

mem.t: Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

lessons.title: Thirty Seconds at the Coffee Machine
lessons.theme: Seize each brief encounter, and let your words carry grace

v: Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving,
praying together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds,
that I may reveal it as I ought to speak.
Walk in wisdom towards those who are outside, redeeming the time.
Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

lessons.still: As you step into the lift, pray for thirty seconds: “Lord, open a door for the word today. Help me notice the brief encounters, and let my speech be full of grace, as if seasoned with salt.”
teach: When Paul wrote Colossians he was in chains. He did not first ask the believers to pray for his release; he asked that God would “open to us a door for the word.” Then he turned to the believers themselves: “Walk in wisdom towards those who are outside, redeeming the time.” “Redeeming the time” carries the sense of buying back the opportunity. Paul knew that the door for the gospel is often not a great gate but a series of small windows in everyday life.

At an airport gate there is a boarding window: open for twenty minutes, and once it closes, the plane leaves. Gospel opportunities at work are often like that, lasting only a few minutes—waiting for coffee in the pantry, riding the lift from the ground floor to the twelfth, walking to the car park after working late. Wisdom is noticing these windows opening rather than missing them with eyes on our phones. Speech full of grace need not be a sermon; it might simply be a sincere “How have you really been?”

Speech “seasoned with salt” is neither bland small talk nor a stinging lecture; it has flavour and proportion, and makes people want to keep listening. That starts with prayer: Paul says, “Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving.” Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself. When prayer fills me with God's love, my words naturally carry grace; when I'm just trying to complete an “evangelism task,” my words turn stiff. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—it applies here too.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God, self, others, tasks. Connect with God in prayer first, then with people through gracious words. People matter more than tasks: colleagues are not my evangelism targets but people God loves.
lessons.scene: Yixuan is a copywriter at an advertising agency in Taipei. This afternoon in the pantry, Kelly, a designer who usually seems unflappable, says quietly while waiting for coffee, “I've been sleeping less than four hours a night. This job feels so empty.” The machine will finish in thirty seconds, and both of them have meetings straight after. Something stirs in Yixuan's heart.
q: Who is God? — In chains, Paul still asked God to “open to us a door for the word.” What kind of door-opening God do you see?
Who am I? — Is your speech more often bland small talk, a stinging lecture, or grace “seasoned with salt”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yixuan, what would you say in those thirty seconds at the coffee machine?
lessons.jesus: Hurrying through a crowd to save Jairus' daughter, Jesus stopped and asked, “Who touched my clothes?” (Mark 5:30). He never treated interruptions as wasted time; he saw the one person in the crowd who needed him. He redeemed the time not for the sake of a schedule but out of love.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for a new day and the many brief encounters it holds. Open my eyes to the people who need care—in the pantry, in the lift, before and after meetings. Let my speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, neither bland nor stinging. Give me a door today, and the courage to walk through it. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: In one brief encounter, sincerely ask after a colleague
Before speaking, pray silently: “Lord, season my words”
While waiting, put your phone away and notice people
lessons.noon: “Let your speech always be with grace” — Lord, right now let every word I say carry kindness.

lessons.title: Give Me a Drink
lessons.theme: Jesus began with need, not with condemnation

v: A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”
For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.
The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”
The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming, he who is called Christ. When he has come, he will declare to us all things.”
Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.”

lessons.still: Before you leave, pick up your water bottle, take a sip, and be still for thirty seconds. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you are the spring of living water. Today let me, like you, open a door to you in an ordinary conversation.”
teach: At the well at midday a Samaritan woman came to draw water. Jesus opened neither with a sermon nor with her past. He said, “Give me a drink.” She was astonished: “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” For “Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.” With one small request Jesus crossed the walls of ethnicity and reputation. Then he moved the conversation from well water to “living water,” and finally said, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.”

A good doctor doesn't sit down and write a prescription straight away. First he asks, “Where does it hurt? How long has it been?” He starts with what the patient feels and works step by step towards the cause. Jesus did the same at the well: he began with thirst, went on to the deeper thirst of the heart, and pointed to himself as the only one who satisfies it. A gospel conversation at work doesn't need to open with a set of doctrines. It can begin with someone's thirst—weariness at work, hurt in relationships, the search for meaning—and slowly go deeper.

Jesus was willing to ask something of someone; that itself is humility. We often think we must be the givers before we can share the gospel, yet sometimes asking a colleague to show you a piece of software, borrowing a pen, or asking for a restaurant recommendation is what opens a conversation. Humility is laying down power and returning to your proper place, and humility draws out humility. When we don't stand on high but sit by the well, people are willing to open their hearts to us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example—he set aside his status and sat by a well asking for water. The focus is on the other person's need, and on Jesus who meets it, not on my performance. Humility is returning to my proper place.
lessons.scene: Isaac works as a claims officer at an insurance company in Wellington. At lunch he spots Tama from his team sitting in his car in the car park, not getting out, eyes red. Last week everyone heard that Tama's divorce had just gone through. Isaac is still holding his own lunch, wondering whether to knock on the window.
q: Who is God? — Jesus spoke first to the Samaritan woman. What does this show you about how he sees people others avoid?
Who am I? — Do you usually start conversations from the other person's “need” or from “doctrine”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Isaac, after knocking on the window, what would your first words be?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “being tired from his journey, sat down by the well” (John 4:6). He was truly weary and truly thirsty. The giver of living water asked a woman for a drink. Later, on the cross, he said, “I am thirsty!” (John 19:28). He thirsted so that we need never thirst again. The conversation at the well is the gospel in miniature: first he stoops to us, then he gives himself to us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for waiting at the well for that woman, and waiting for me in the dry places of my life. Keep me from sharing the gospel from on high; make me willing to sit beside my colleagues, hear their thirst, and walk a little way with them. If I meet someone in need today, give me a simple, gentle first sentence. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Ask a colleague for help with something small today
Notice someone who seems tired or low
Start a conversation with “Are you all right?”
lessons.noon: “Give me a drink” — Lord, right now help me lay down my pride and begin with the other person's need.

lessons.title: Levi's Dinner Table
lessons.theme: Bring your industry peers to Jesus, beginning with a meal

v: After these things he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax office, and said to him, “Follow me!”
He left everything, and rose up and followed him.
Levi made a great feast for him in his house. There was a great crowd of tax collectors and others who were reclining with them.
Their scribes and the Pharisees murmured against his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with the tax collectors and sinners?”
Jesus answered them, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do.
I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.”

lessons.still: Before you go out, think of the colleagues or industry peers you've eaten with recently. Be still for thirty seconds and tell the Lord: “Lord, my table is your table. Let the people around me meet you at my table.”
teach: Levi was a tax collector, “sitting at the tax office.” To Jews of the time, tax collectors gathered money for Rome and often overcharged to line their own pockets; they were unwelcome. Jesus said to him, “Follow me!” and Levi “left everything, and rose up and followed him.” The first thing he did next was to make “a great feast for him in his house,” inviting “a great crowd of tax collectors and others.” He didn't rush to cut off his old friends; he brought them to Jesus.

Many companies have a year-end dinner or team meal. The people around that round table may not be your favourites, but they are the ones you labour alongside every day. Levi's feast was an “industry round table”: everyone there did the same work and understood each other's struggles. You don't need to host a big evangelistic event. A birthday meal, a housewarming, Friday drinks after work—any of these can become Levi's feast. What matters is not how lavish the food is, but whether Jesus is at the table—through your laughter, your grace before meals, your care.

The Pharisees grumbled, “Why do you eat and drink with the tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus answered, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do.” Self-centred faith wants to stay clean and away from sinners; the self-emptied life walks into the crowd as Jesus did. People matter more than tasks, relationships more than things; a relationship built over a meal may be someone's first step towards Jesus. Of course, as we go among people, we keep our boundaries in the Spirit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 235 starts with real relationships. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—Levi first followed Jesus, then used his relationships to bring his peers to Jesus. Relationships are the channel through which the gospel flows.
lessons.scene: Yongfu runs a used-car dealership in Kuala Lumpur and was baptised last month. With Chinese New Year approaching, he wants to hold an open house and invite several dealers from the area for a meal. But they swear once they've had a few drinks, and church friends have warned him, “Stop hanging around with those people.” He looks at his guest list, pen hovering.
q: Who is God? — “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.” What does this show you about Jesus' heart?
Who am I? — Are you afraid of getting too close to “those people”? What are you really afraid of?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yongfu, how would you host this meal—inviting your peers while keeping your boundaries?
lessons.jesus: People called Jesus “a gluttonous man and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matthew 11:19). It was meant as an accusation, but it became one of the loveliest descriptions of the gospel. He was not afraid to soil his reputation, because he came to be a physician. We can sit at God's feast today only because he first came and sat at the table of sinners like us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for being a friend of sinners, and a friend to me. Rescue me from a spiritual fastidiousness that fears contamination, and make me like Levi, bringing my colleagues and peers to you. Guard my words and my boundaries at the table, so that people in my home and at my table taste your grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: List three colleagues or peers you could invite to a meal
This week, arrange a meal with one of them
Before eating, ask: “I usually say grace—do you mind?”
lessons.noon: “Follow me!” — Lord, right now I choose to follow you, and to bring others to you.

lessons.title: Read the Error Message First
lessons.theme: Understand the question, then answer faith's hard questions gently

v: Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things.
For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you.
The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands.
He isn’t served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath and all things.
He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings,
that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us.
The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all, able to teach, patient,
in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,

lessons.still: Before you open your laptop, be silent for thirty seconds. Tell the Lord: “Lord, if anyone asks me a hard question about faith today, help me first understand their heart. Keep me from needing to win; let me point to you with gentleness and reverence.”
teach: In Athens Paul was troubled to see a city full of idols. Yet when he stood on the Areopagus, he did not open with “You're all worshipping wrongly.” He began, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things.” He started from an altar inscribed “TO AN UNKNOWN GOD,” from his hearers' own world, and spoke of the God who made the world, who “is not far from each one of us.” Paul observed and understood first; only then did he answer.

When a program crashes, an engineer's first move is not to start changing code at random but to read the error message: which line failed, and why? It's the same when colleagues ask questions about faith. “Why do good people suffer?” may hide the pain of a recent bereavement. “Aren't Christians really exclusive?” may hide the wound of being judged by a believer. Ask first, “What makes you think about that?” Only by reading the error message can you find the line that truly needs answering.

Paul taught Timothy, “The Lord's servant must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all, able to teach, patient.” Answering faith questions is not a debating contest. The self-centred want to win, and end up winning the argument but losing the person. The self-emptied simply want the other person to see Jesus, and can even say, “I'm still learning about that too—shall we look for answers together?” Pride provokes pride; humility draws out humility. Gentleness and reverence are themselves the strongest answer.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is the key to revival. In answering faith questions, the focus is not proving myself right but letting Jesus be King. Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself: understanding people matters more than out-arguing them.
lessons.scene: Pinrui is a process engineer at a semiconductor plant in Hsinchu. At a team dinner after work, a senior colleague who's had a few drinks suddenly asks, “Do you Christians think people like me who burn incense at the temple are going to hell?” The table falls silent; someone laughs awkwardly. Pinrui knows this is more than a question—the colleague's grandmother died just last month.
q: Who is God? — Paul says God “is not far from each one of us.” What does this show you about how God seeks people?
Who am I? — Faced with hard questions about faith, do you want more to “win” or to “let people see Jesus”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Pinrui, what would you first ask your colleague, and how would you answer gently?
lessons.jesus: A lawyer tested Jesus: “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus replied, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?” (Luke 10:25–26). He often answered questions with questions, leading people to look into their own hearts. He was not afraid of hard questions, nor in a hurry to win; what he wanted was the person's heart.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for answering my questions so patiently when I didn't yet understand. When colleagues ask me about faith, help me first understand their hearts, not rush to argue, and not be afraid to say “I don't know.” Give me gentleness, reverence and wisdom, so that my answers carry your grace and point to your cross. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When asked about faith, first ask: “What makes you think that?”
Write down the faith question you most dread
Ask a mature believer how they would answer it
lessons.noon: “he is not far from each one of us” — Lord, right now I trust that you are not far from my colleagues either.

lessons.title: Three Pinned Names
lessons.theme: Evangelism begins in prayer: bring three colleagues before God

v: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men,
for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence.
For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour,
who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.
Brothers, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God is for Israel, that they may be saved.

lessons.still: Before you go out, slowly say the names of three colleagues in your heart, pausing after each. Tell the Lord: “Lord, you desire all people to be saved, and you desire them to be saved. Today I bring them to you.”
teach: Paul urged Timothy: “I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men.” Why “first of all” prayer? Because God “desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.” In Romans Paul also writes, “my heart's desire and my prayer to God is for Israel, that they may be saved.” Paul was a great missionary, but his mission always began with prayer. Only God can open a human heart; our prayer is knocking at God's door.

Messaging apps have a “pin” feature: you fix the most important conversation at the top, and however many new messages flood in, it never gets buried. Today, pin three colleagues' names at the top of your prayers. Not vague prayers for everyone, but specific prayers for these three names, their families and their pressures. Keep it up for a while and you'll find you see them differently—prayer often changes us first.

This is the practice of 920: every person connected to me is one of my “2”. I intercede for them in prayer and live out the self-emptied “0” before them in daily life, so that the “9”, the fruit of the Spirit, grows in those relationships. The last of the eight steps is multiplication; today's three names may one day become your spiritual companions, even your spiritual children. This week has moved from the coffee machine, the well, the feast and the hard questions to the most basic place of all: prayer.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 920—every colleague is one of my “2”. Pray for them before God first, then give yourself for them before people. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: this is where building God's order begins.
lessons.scene: Cuilan teaches Chinese at a primary school in Guangzhou. This week three colleagues in her teaching group are each struggling: the group leader's child faces the university entrance exam and the whole family is on edge; a new teacher has had a complaint from a parent; the teacher next door often says she “believes in nothing but herself.” On the last page of her lesson planner Cuilan writes three names, wondering whom to pray for first.
q: Who is God? — “who desires all people to be saved.” What does this show you about God's heart for your colleagues?
Who am I? — When did you last pray for a colleague by name?
How shall I respond? — If you were Cuilan, how would you pray for each of these three? What could you do for them today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus told Peter, “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn't fail” (Luke 22:32). Before Peter knew he would fall, Jesus had already prayed for him by name. Today the risen Lord is at the right hand of God and “makes intercession for us” (Romans 8:34). When we pray for our colleagues, we join Jesus' own intercession.
lessons.pray: Father, you desire all people to be saved and come to know the truth. Today I bring three colleagues before you by name (say their names). Watch over their families, their work and their inner struggles, and reveal yourself to them in your good time. Make me a channel of your love beside them. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write three colleagues' names and pin them in your phone
Pray specifically for each name for a minute today
Do one small act of service for one of them
lessons.noon: “who desires all people to be saved” — Lord, right now I pray to you for those three names.

mem.t: with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints.

lessons.title: Know Your Real Opponent
lessons.theme: Colleagues are not the enemy; the powers of darkness behind them are

v: Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.
Put on the whole armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.

For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world’s rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.
Therefore put on the whole armour of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.

lessons.still: Before you start work, breathe deeply for thirty seconds and think of the person most likely to give you a headache today. Tell the Lord: “Lord, they are not my enemy. Help me stand in your mighty strength against the real enemy, not attack the people around me.”
teach: Paul opens the last section of Ephesians with “Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.” Then he uncovers a fact we easily forget: “our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world's rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” Wrestling is close-quarters combat. Every day believers are in an unseen struggle, and the opponent is not people.

A firefighter going into a burning building never fights the people trapped inside. His opponent is the fire, not the people; those who panic and even push him away are the very ones he has come to save. Work is the same. The colleague who takes your credit, the manager who changes their mind every week, the customer who makes unreasonable demands—none of them is your real enemy. The real enemy is the one who sets fires in human hearts through pride, envy, bitterness and lies. Mistake the enemy, and we turn the hose on people while the fire keeps burning.

This doesn't mean injustice at work is unimportant, or that we blame everything on the devil. Unfair treatment still needs to be addressed in proper ways, and if you face bullying or illegal demands, seek help from someone you trust or from professionals. But in our hearts we must discern: the enemy's favourite scheme is to stir up our self-centredness—the urge to retaliate, to prove ourselves, to take control. Pride is the root of the fall; humility is the key to revival. Being strong in the Lord means lowering our fists before people and lifting our hands before God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-centredness is the root of the fall, and the enemy's favourite point of attack. The focus is on Jesus, not on others: don't hurt people for the sake of a task; stand in the Lord's mighty strength against the real enemy.
lessons.scene: Ziqing is a customer service manager at a bank in Kuala Lumpur. This morning she learned that the manager of the neighbouring team presented, at a senior management meeting, the process improvements her team spent three months on as his own. Furious, she has typed a long email, copying in every senior manager, and the cursor is resting on “Send.”
q: Who is God? — Paul says to be strong “in the strength of his might.” What does this show you about who God is in your battles?
Who am I? — At work, whom do you most often treat as your “enemy”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Ziqing, before pressing send, how would you discern the real enemy and handle this properly?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane a disciple drew his sword and cut off the high priest's servant's ear, but Jesus said, “Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). He knew the real battle was not fought with swords but on the cross. There, not by violence but by obedience, he triumphed over the principalities and powers.
lessons.pray: Lord, open my eyes to see that my real enemy is not my colleague, my manager or my customer. When I am wronged or my credit is taken, guard my heart from bitterness and help me stand firm in your mighty strength. Give me wisdom, too, to deal with unfairness in the right way. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray once for the person giving you the biggest headache
Save any angry email as a draft; reread it in an hour
Name the bitterness in your heart to God and hand it over
lessons.noon: “be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might” — Lord, right now I lean not on my anger but on you.

lessons.title: Safety Gear Before Site Entry
lessons.theme: Each workday, first put on the whole armour God gives

v: Stand therefore, having the utility belt of truth buckled around your waist, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness,
and having fitted your feet with the preparation of the Good News of peace,
above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one.
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God;
But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.

lessons.still: As you put on your jacket or lanyard, pause for thirty seconds and name each piece to the Lord: “I buckle on truth, put on righteousness, step into peace, take up faith, put on salvation, and take up your word.” Then head out.
teach: Paul wrote this letter in chains, perhaps with a Roman soldier standing guard beside him. He used the soldier's kit to picture the believer's armour: the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, feet fitted with the Good News of peace, the shield of faith that can “quench all the fiery darts of the evil one,” the helmet of salvation, and “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” Of the six pieces, the first five are mostly for defence; only one—the word of God—is a weapon for going on the attack.

At the entrance to a building site there is usually a sign: “No hard hat, no hi-vis, no safety boots—no entry.” Even the most experienced tradesman doesn't say, “I know this site well; I don't need it,” because accidents never give notice. Spiritual armour is the same. Truth is the belt: tell one lie and the whole kit comes loose. Righteousness is the breastplate, guarding our hearts from being pierced by guilt. The peace of the gospel is the safety boots that keep us steady on slippery ground. Every day, kit up before entering the site.

This armour is not something we make; it is “the whole armour of God.” Truth, righteousness, peace and salvation are, in the end, Jesus himself. Elsewhere Paul says, “put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14). Putting on the whole armour means clothing ourselves with Christ again each morning. This is the self-emptied life: no longer I, but Christ living in me. We don't get through the day on willpower; we get through it by the Lord we have put on.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard—the word of God is our weapon for advance. The self-emptied life is putting on Christ: not relying on my own armour, but Christ living in me as my truth, righteousness and peace.
lessons.scene: Hemi is the safety officer for a construction firm in Christchurch. This morning the main contractor's project manager walks over with a stack of safety checklists: “The scaffolding isn't fully inspected yet, but the client's coming to look this afternoon. Just sign now—I promise we'll finish it tomorrow.” The crew are waiting to start, and Hemi's pen is already touching the paper.
q: Who is God? — The armour is “of God.” What does this show you about how God equips his children?
Who am I? — Of the six pieces, which do you most often “forget to put on”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Hemi, how would you respond to the project manager, holding to truth while respecting the schedule?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he didn't fight back with miracles but answered with Scripture: “For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only’” (Matthew 4:10). He took up the very sword of the Spirit. He himself is the truth, our righteousness and our peace; every piece of armour we wear is something he has prepared for us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, be my armour today. Buckle your truth around me, so that I am honest in every signature, report and promise. Guard my heart with your righteousness, and steady my steps with your peace. When pressure tempts me to cut corners, remind me of your word and help me stand. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before leaving, name the six pieces of armour
Refuse one small “sign now, sort it later” compromise
Memorise one verse as today's sword
lessons.noon: “put on the Lord Jesus Christ” — Lord, right now I rely not on my own armour but put on you.

lessons.title: The Radio That Stays On
lessons.theme: Pray at all times in the Spirit, staying connected through the workday

v: with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints.
Pray for me, that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Good News,
for which I am an ambassador in chains; that in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.

lessons.still: On your commute, put your phone on silent for thirty seconds. Tell the Lord: “Lord, however many meetings and emails today brings, my heart stays open to you. Holy Spirit, remind me to talk with you all day long.”
teach: Having described the whole armour, Paul doesn't say, “Right, off to battle.” He goes on: “with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints.” Prayer is like the power that makes the whole armour work. Paul then asks the believers to pray for him: “that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Good News.” Even an apostle needed others' prayers in order to speak boldly.

In hospitals, on building sites and at big events, staff often wear a two-way radio. It isn't switched on only when needed; the channel stays open all day, so they can call in at any moment and control can give instructions at any time. “Praying at all times” is like that radio: not just a long prayer morning and evening, but a channel open all day—“Lord, give me wisdom” before a meeting, “Lord, guard my mouth” before replying to an email, “Lord, help me forgive” after being shouted at.

Many people say, “I'm too busy at work to pray.” But praying at all times isn't adding extra time; it's handing our time to God. Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself; the heart brings joy, the head brings worry. When we stay connected to God all day, we don't have to carry everything alone. Paul also says to pray “for all the saints”: pray for other Christians in your company, and become spiritual companions and comrades in 235, speaking boldly for the Lord at work together.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide—praying at all times in the Spirit lets him guide every working moment. Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself; keep your focus on Jesus, not on the pressure.
lessons.scene: Haoran is a senior consultant at a foreign consultancy in Shanghai. His calendar holds seven meetings today, and the first is to tell a notoriously difficult client that the project is delayed. Two minutes before the video call, his heart is pounding, and the last slide of his deck still isn't finished.
q: Who is God? — Paul speaks of praying “in the Spirit.” What does this show you about the Spirit's role in your workday?
Who am I? — Is your prayer life more like a radio “switched on when needed” or one with “the channel open all day”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Haoran, how would you pray in the two minutes before the meeting?
lessons.jesus: As word about Jesus spread and crowds flocked to him from everywhere, Scripture says, “But he withdrew himself into the desert and prayed” (Luke 5:16). The busier he was, the more he prayed. His connection with the Father was never broken; even on the cross, his last words were spoken to the Father. Our prayer life follows in his footsteps.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, remind me to pray at all times today. Before meetings, before calls, when pressure mounts, keep my heart open to you like a radio that never switches off. Remember the other brothers and sisters in my company, too; help us pray for one another and speak boldly for the Lord together. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before each meeting, pray silently: “Lord, give me wisdom”
Swap prayer requests with a Christian colleague
Pray today for a colleague's gospel opportunity
lessons.noon: “praying at all times in the Spirit” — Lord, right now my heart is open to you.

lessons.title: The Choir in Front of the Army
