lessons.theme: When we don't know what to do, we turn our eyes to God first

v: Our God, will you not judge them? For we have no might against this great company that comes against us. We don’t know what to do, but our eyes are on you.”

When he had taken counsel with the people, he appointed those who were to sing to the LORD and give praise in holy array as they go out before the army, and say, “Give thanks to the LORD, for his loving kindness endures forever.”
When they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushers against the children of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, who had come against Judah; and they were struck.

lessons.still: Before you leave, sing a line of a familiar hymn, or quietly repeat for thirty seconds: “Give thanks to the LORD, for his loving kindness endures forever.” Then place today's biggest problem in the Lord's hands.
teach: When Moab, Ammon and their allies came against Judah, King Jehoshaphat “was alarmed.” He didn't pretend to be brave; he set himself to seek the LORD and proclaimed a fast throughout the land. His prayer was utterly honest: “We have no might against this great company that comes against us. We don't know what to do, but our eyes are on you.” God answered through a prophet: “the battle is not yours, but God's.” The next day Jehoshaphat made a militarily absurd decision: he appointed singers to go out before the army, praising the LORD.

Many companies' crisis meetings begin with chart after falling chart, and the anxiety grows with each one. Imagine a manager changing item one on the agenda to: “Five minutes to name what we are still thankful for.” That isn't denial; it's recalibrating our view. Jehoshaphat's choir was item one on the agenda: declaring God's love before seeing any victory. And “when they began to sing and to praise, the LORD set ambushers” against the enemy. Praise is not the celebration after victory but faith before it.

Praise is a posture of humility: I admit I am powerless and don't know what to do, but I know who God is. Humility is laying down power and returning to your proper place, letting people be people and God be God. Jehoshaphat laid down his urge to control the battle and returned to his place of looking to God. In a workplace crisis we still do our part: plan, communicate, and where needed seek professional financial or legal advice. But our hearts can stand first in the place of praise.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility means laying down power and returning to your proper place. When Jehoshaphat said, “We don't know what to do,” he let God be God. Shift perspective: from the earthly crisis to the heavenly Lord whose loving kindness endures forever.
lessons.scene: Jia Hui runs an eight-person design studio in Singapore. Yesterday her biggest client suddenly pulled out—forty per cent of the year's revenue—and there is only two months' cash in the bank. At nine tomorrow morning she must hold an all-staff meeting, and everyone has already heard the rumours. Sitting in the empty studio, she has no idea how to begin.
q: Who is God? — “The battle is not yours, but God's.” What does this show you about who God is in your crisis?
Who am I? — When you “don't know what to do,” what is your first reaction?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jia Hui, how would you open tomorrow morning's meeting?
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus knew the cross lay just ahead. Yet Scripture records: “When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 26:30). He led his disciples, singing, towards Gethsemane and the cross. Jesus is the worship leader who goes before the army, carrying praise into the darkest battlefield—and winning.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess today's problem is bigger than I am, and I don't know what to do, but my eyes are on you. Before I see any way out, help me give thanks to you, for your loving kindness endures forever. Give me wisdom to do my part, and peace to leave the outcome with you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down three things you can still thank God for today
Before a hard meeting, silently speak one line of praise
Write your biggest problem on paper and pray it over to God
lessons.noon: “We don't know what to do, but our eyes are on you” — Lord, right now I don't know what to do, but I look to you.

lessons.title: Ten Minutes at the Terminus
lessons.theme: Build a steady rhythm of prayer into the workday

v: When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room towards Jerusalem) and he knelt on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.
Evening, morning, and at noon, I will cry out in distress. He will hear my voice.

lessons.still: This morning, first set three reminders on your phone: morning, midday and late afternoon. Then be still for thirty seconds and tell the Lord: “Lord, let these three times be my appointments with you.”
teach: Daniel knew the decree had been signed: for thirty days, anyone praying to any god but the king would be thrown into the lions' den. Yet he went home and “knelt on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.” The key is in the last words: “as he did before.” He didn't start praying in the crisis; he already had a steady rhythm, and when the crisis came, the rhythm became his strength. The psalmist says too: “Evening, morning, and at noon, I will cry out in distress. He will hear my voice.”

After every run, a bus driver stops at the terminus for ten minutes: a drink of water, a toilet break, adjusting the seat, then off on the next run. Without those ten minutes, even the best driver ends up driving tired. A prayer rhythm in the workday is like those ten minutes at the terminus: before leaving in the morning, entrust the day to God; at the lunch break, recalibrate your direction; before heading home, lay down the day's burdens. It isn't an extra burden but a refuelling stop that lets us go further.

This week we have learned about spiritual warfare at work: knowing the real enemy, putting on the armour, praying at all times, meeting battles with praise. All of it finally needs to settle into a simple rhythm. Among the eight steps for changing our mindset are “practice and repetition”—spiritual strength comes not from one moving moment but from daily training. Starting today, build your workday rhythm of prayer, so that prayer becomes as natural as breathing and Jesus is King in every part of your working day.
lessons.light: 321 Light: “Practice and repetition” from the eight steps—a prayer rhythm turns faith into daily living. Life first, then living; when prayer becomes “as he did before,” we let Jesus be King in every part of the working day.
lessons.scene: Guohua has driven buses in Tainan for twelve years, running the same route six times a day. He often says he has “no time to read the Bible or pray”: out at five in the morning, home at night and straight to bed. Today at noon, at the terminus, he sits in the empty bus scrolling his phone, waiting for his next departure, and suddenly remembers the pastor's words last week: “as he did before.” He has ten minutes left.
q: Who is God? — “He will hear my voice.” What does this show you about how God responds to our regular prayers?
Who am I? — In your workday, is there a prayer time that happens “as before,” day in, day out?
How shall I respond? — If you were Guohua, how would you use ten minutes at the terminus? Where is your own “terminus”?
lessons.jesus: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). The night before, the whole town had gathered at the door and he had healed many; yet early next morning he met with the Father first. Jesus' strength came from steady, intimate fellowship with the Father.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for hearing my voice morning, noon and night. Help me build a rhythm of prayer into my workday, not from the pressure of rules but from love for you. In every break, let me come back to you; and when crisis comes, let my prayer go on “as I did before.” In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Set three prayer reminders: morning, noon, evening
At lunch today, pray for three minutes, phone down
Before leaving work, thank God for today's work
lessons.noon: “He will hear my voice” — Lord, right now, in this break from work, I come to you.

mem.t: The things which you have heard from me amongst many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

lessons.title: Paul and Timothy: Father and Son in the Faith
lessons.theme: Faith is not only taught; it is passed on through companionship

v: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
The things which you have heard from me amongst many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
to Timothy, my true child in faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

lessons.still: Before work, place a hand on your chest and be still for thirty seconds. Think of someone who once walked a stretch of the road with you, and thank God for them. Then say: “Lord, someone once walked with me. Today, let me walk with someone else.”
teach: When Paul met Timothy at Lystra, he was simply a young disciple of whom the brothers “gave a good testimony” (Acts 16:2). Paul took him along: on the road, through persecution, into the planting of churches. Years later Paul wrote to “Timothy, my true child in faith” — not a bond of blood, yet deeper than blood. Near the end of his life he urged him: “The things which you have heard from me amongst many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.” One verse holds four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others.

Most companies have a thick handover manual, yet new staff rarely learn the job from the manual. They learn it from the colleague at the next desk who says, “Here, let me show you once.” A manual can record a process but not judgement; it can list the procedure but not the gentleness and firmness of someone handling an angry customer. God’s Kingdom is handed on the same way. Truth needs words, but it also needs a living person who lets you watch those words being lived. Paul gave Timothy more than lecture notes; he gave him years of shared life.

Paul begins: “You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” Spiritual parenting does not start with being mature or flawless; it starts with standing firm in grace. When the self-centred life mentors others, it produces copies or fans of itself. The self-emptied life brings people to Christ. Change your thinking and your life changes: the workplace is not only where I am fed, but where I commit to others what I have received. In these last four weeks of the year, we turn from learners into companions.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The “3” in 235 is the spiritual parent–child relationship. Life first, then relationship, then ministry: Paul lived it before Timothy, then entrusted the work to him. God’s order is multiplied, generation by generation, in grace.
lessons.scene: Dexing has managed a precision-machinery plant in Taichung for twenty years and retires in two. One evening a young engineer catches him in the car park: “Sir, the client tore into you today. How can you be so calm?” Car keys in hand, Dexing hesitates over whether to say, “Free next week? Let’s grab a coffee.”
q: Who is God? — When Paul calls Timothy his “true child”, what do you see about a God who values relationship?
Who am I? — Looking back on your journey of faith, who has been your “Paul”? Have you been anyone’s “Paul”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Dexing, how would you answer the young engineer’s question?
lessons.jesus: Jesus appointed the twelve first of all “that they might be with him” (Mark 3:14), and only then sent them out to preach. He did not run a course, hand out notes and leave. He ate, walked and wept with them; he laid down his life for them and sent the Spirit to keep walking with them. Every pattern of spiritual parenting flows from the Lord who first walked with us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you never treat me as a project, but walk with me as your child. Thank you for the brothers and sisters who prayed for me in pantries and outside meeting rooms. Make me strong in your grace — not leaning on my seniority, not wanting to copy myself — but longing to bring the young colleagues around me to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Message someone who helped you grow and thank them
Write down the name of a young colleague you might walk with
Set 2 Timothy 2:2 as your phone wallpaper today
lessons.noon: “be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” — Lord, right now I lean not on my experience but on your grace.

lessons.title: Find a Fellow Traveller
lessons.theme: Two by two is how the Lord sends his people

v: Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he was about to come.
Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the labourers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out labourers into his harvest.
Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.

lessons.still: Breathe in deeply and let it out slowly. Picture Jesus standing beside you and say: “Lord, you send people out two by two. Open my eyes today to see the fellow traveller you have prepared for me.”
teach: Jesus sent out the seventy not one by one but “two by two”. In an age without phones or maps, two could bear witness together, protect each other and hold each other up. Solomon says, “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.” A spiritual companion is not someone who only says “You’ve got this!” but someone who sharpens you — sometimes gently, sometimes painfully, always so that you become more like Christ.

At the gym, any trainer will tell you that once the bench press gets heavy, you need a spotter behind you. He doesn’t touch the bar most of the time; he only steps in at the moment you can’t push it up. A spiritual companion at work is like that. He won’t do your job or make your decisions. But when your manager humiliates you in front of everyone and you want to hit back, or when your finger hovers over “send” on a dishonest email, someone asks: “Shall we pray first?”

The “2” in 235 is a spiritual companion: someone who also wants to live the self-emptied life. The self-centred life looks for people who agree with it; the self-emptied life dares to let someone come close and see its weakness. You need not wait for the perfect person. Two things are enough: they love the Lord, and they will tell you the truth. Life first, then relationship, then ministry — you don’t need a grand plan for the company. Begin with fifteen minutes a week of sharing and prayer.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The “2” in 235 is a spiritual companion. Humility draws out humility: when I admit first that “I need someone”, the other person can lower their guard too. People matter more than tasks, and companionship is the first brick of God’s order at work.
lessons.scene: Qiaolin is a senior auditor at an accounting firm in Singapore. Among the twelve on her team, she has always assumed she is the only Christian. One lunchtime during year-end close she notices a new colleague, Priscilla, bowing her head over her lunch box in the corner. Tray in hand, Qiaolin stops — caught between walking over and pretending not to see.
q: Who is God? — Jesus sends people “two by two”. What does that show you about how he cares for our weakness?
Who am I? — At work, do you usually tough it out alone, or is there someone you can be honest with?
How shall I respond? — If you were Qiaolin, once you walked over, how would you invite Priscilla to be a companion?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus took three disciples and said, “Stay here and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38). The Son of God let others see his sorrow and longed for company. The disciples fell asleep, yet he went on alone to the cross, and became the companion who never dozes off, promising, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that you never send me into battle alone. I confess that I would often rather grit my teeth than let colleagues see my weakness. Please give me a companion who loves you and tells me the truth, and make me that companion for someone else. Through closing deadlines, submissions and late nights, let us sharpen each other and grow more like you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: List two colleagues who love the Lord and speak the truth
Send one of them a message of encouragement today
Invite them to lunch next week and pray together for ten minutes
lessons.noon: “Iron sharpens iron” — Lord, right now give me a companion who sharpens me, and let me be one for someone else.

lessons.title: Like a Mother, Like a Father
lessons.theme: Spiritual parents nurture growth; they do not control lives

v: But we were gentle amongst you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.
Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.
For you remember, brothers, our labour and travail; for working night and day, that we might not burden any of you, we preached to you the Good News of God.
You are witnesses with God how holy, righteously, and blamelessly we behaved ourselves towards you who believe.
As you know, we exhorted, comforted, and implored every one of you, as a father does his own children,
to the end that you should walk worthily of God, who calls you into his own Kingdom and glory.

lessons.still: Unclench your hands and rest them palms up on your knees. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I put down the hands that want to control everything. Every person I lead or care for today is yours, not mine.”
teach: Looking back on his time in Thessalonica, Paul uses two family pictures. First, “we were gentle amongst you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children” — tender and self-giving, ready to share “our own souls”. Then, “as a father does his own children” — exhorting, comforting, imploring. A mother’s tenderness and a father’s guidance, joined together. And Paul was “working night and day, that we might not burden any of you”. Spiritual parents do not take from people; they give themselves for them.

A bonsai artist wraps wire tightly around each branch and forces it into the shape he wants. A gardener waters, feeds and puts in a stake, so the tree can grow tall the way God made it. Some managers train people like bonsai: do it my way, live at my pace — even your evenings are my business. A spiritual parent is a gardener. They bring nourishment and stand with you through the storm season, but growth belongs to God, and the direction is Christ, not me.

Paul’s aim is clear: “that you should walk worthily of God, who calls you into his own Kingdom and glory.” Worthy of God — not worthy of me. Self-centred spiritual parents slowly start to rule in their children’s lives, putting themselves in God’s place. Self-emptied spiritual parents let people be people and let God be God. Control makes people depend more and more on you; companionship makes them depend more and more on God. The truest success for a spiritual parent is the day the child needs you less and follows the Lord more closely.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility means laying down power and returning to my proper place. The great temptation of a spiritual parent is to be king in someone else’s life. Letting Jesus be King includes letting him reign — not me — in the lives of those I walk with.
lessons.scene: Xiuzhu manages a branch of a bakery chain in Kuala Lumpur. Weijie, a nineteen-year-old on her staff, came to faith recently, but has been late twice this week — gaming until the small hours, she hears. She is tempted to call him in and require a text by eleven every night, and a photo every Sunday to prove he went to church. She picks up the walkie-talkie, then puts it down.
q: Who is God? — Through the images of mother and father, what do you see about how God treats his children?
Who am I? — When you lead people, are you more like the bonsai artist with his wire, or the gardener with his watering can?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiuzhu, how would you talk with Weijie with both a father’s charge and a mother’s gentleness?
lessons.jesus: When the rich young man came asking about eternal life, “Jesus looking at him loved him” (Mark 10:21). He told him the truth — and let him walk away sorrowful. Jesus did not chase him, lower the bar or manipulate his heart. He gives his life for people, yet honours their response. In him we see perfect love and perfect freedom.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for nurturing me as tenderly as a mother and guiding me as patiently as a father. I confess that I often want to control the people I lead and mould them by my standards. Take away the part of me that wants to be king. Let me walk with people without manipulating them, speak the truth without condemning, and hand them back to you again and again. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one strength of someone you lead
Ask them one question today, and listen before advising
Pray for them for one minute and entrust them to God
lessons.noon: “like a nursing mother cherishes her own children” — Lord, right now give me a gentle heart, not a controlling hand.

lessons.title: The Operating Theatre Team
lessons.theme: God gives different gifts so we can build up Christ’s body together at work

v: He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers;
for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ,
until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,

lessons.still: Open your hand and look at your five fingers: different lengths, one hand. Say: “Lord, thank you that you don’t need me to be good at everything. Today let me see my companions’ gifts and gladly do my own part.”
teach: The ascended Christ gave gifts: “some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers.” Apostles pioneer, prophets discern direction, evangelists bring people to Christ, shepherds care for the flock, teachers explain the truth. The goal is not for a few to perform, but “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ”. These five are not merely titles; they are five ways of bringing people to maturity, until we reach “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ”.

An operation is never a one-surgeon show. The anaesthetist watches the vital signs, the scrub nurse passes the instruments, the circulating nurse keeps the whole theatre running, so the surgeon can concentrate on the incision. If anyone is missing, the patient is at risk; if anyone tries to do it all, things go wrong. A spiritual team at work is the same. One person loves starting new groups; another senses the culture of the office keenly; another talks about faith with colleagues quite naturally; another is good at caring for the wounded; another can make the truth wonderfully clear.

The “5” in 235 is a team of spiritual comrades with five-fold gifts. The self-centred life wants to be the all-round hero, or looks down on people who are different. The self-emptied life knows “I am only one part of the body”, so it gladly fills gaps and gladly admires others. Pride provokes pride, and the team loses on every side; humility draws out humility, and everyone wins. Today, don’t ask, “How do I get everything done?” Ask, “Whom has God placed beside me to finish his work together?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The “5” in 235 is a team of comrades with five-fold gifts. Building God’s order is not a one-man superhero show; it is each one doing their part and building up the others, so that Jesus receives all the glory.
lessons.scene: Stephen heads the IT department of a hospital in Auckland and leads a Wednesday lunchtime gathering of five Christian staff. Lately he has been doing everything himself — booking the room, leading the study, visiting sick colleagues — and he is tired enough to shut it down. Anna, a nurse, messages that she would like to take on pastoral care; Wenjie, a pharmacist, offers to share the Bible study. Stephen stares at his phone, unsure whether to let go.
q: Who is God? — Christ gives many different gifts. What does that show you about his heart for a team?
Who am I? — Among the five gifts, do you feel most like an apostle, a prophet, an evangelist, a shepherd or a teacher?
How shall I respond? — If you were Stephen, how would you reply to Anna and Wenjie?
lessons.jesus: Jesus could have done everything alone, yet he chose a very mixed group: impulsive Peter, doubting Thomas, Matthew the former tax collector, Simon the Zealot. He put them together and commanded them to “love one another” (John 13:34). He is the head and we are the members; a team is united not because personalities match, but because all belong to him.
lessons.pray: Ascended Lord, thank you for giving different gifts to your body. Forgive me for so often trying to carry everything alone, and for looking down on companions who are not like me. In the hospital, the factory and the office, let me see the comrades you have given me. Teach me to let go, to fill gaps and to admire others, as we build a godly team for you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down which of the five gifts fits you best
Affirm a companion’s gift and tell them specifically
Hand over one task you always do yourself
lessons.noon: “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving” — Lord, right now let me gladly do my part and help others do theirs.

lessons.title: The First Coffee Invitation
lessons.theme: Spiritual multiplication begins with one person, one meal, one sincere invitation

v: For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News.
I beg you therefore, be imitators of me.
Because of this I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways which are in Christ, even as I teach everywhere in every assembly.
But you remain in the things which you have learnt and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learnt them.

lessons.still: Open the contacts on your phone and scroll slowly, without doing anything. Say: “Lord, there is a name in here that you want me to walk with. Today, gently light it up in my heart.”
teach: Paul told the Corinthians, “though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers.” There was no shortage of teachers; what was rare was someone willing to pay a father’s price. Paul did not only teach doctrine; he said, “I beg you therefore, be imitators of me.” He sent Timothy to “remind you of my ways which are in Christ”. What is handed down is not only knowledge but “ways”. So he reminds Timothy to remain in what he has learnt, “knowing from whom you have learnt them”.

Have you ever been on a train when a colleague’s phone lost signal, and you switched on your hotspot for them? You don’t need to be a phone company or build a mast. As long as your phone is connected, the person beside you can get online. Walking with a spiritual child is like that. You needn’t be a pastor or have been to seminary. As long as you are connected to Christ, you can share the life you receive from him. What matters is not how strong your signal is, but whether you are willing to switch it on.

How do you begin? First, pray and ask God to show you one person — a new colleague, a seeker at work, a recently converted team member. Second, keep the invitation light and genuine: “Fancy lunch every couple of weeks to talk about work and faith?” Third, listen before you speak: life first, then ministry. Lean on the Spirit with your heart rather than on yourself with your head; don’t rush to “sort them out”, but trust the God who began a good work in them. The one you walk with today will one day walk with someone else — that is the multiplication of 2 Timothy 2:2.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The last of the eight steps is multiplication. One changed life brings change to another; this is the smallest and truest unit of building God’s order.
lessons.scene: Zhiyuan is a product manager at an internet company in Shanghai. Xiaowei, the intern he supervises, has been working until midnight every day. Two days ago, eyes red in the pantry, she said, “I don’t even know what all this striving is for.” Now Zhiyuan opens WeChat and types: “Lunch on Friday? I’d love to hear how you’re really doing.” His thumb hovers over send.
q: Who is God? — Paul “became your father through the Good News”. What does that show you about how God brings spiritual children to birth through people?
Who am I? — Is your way of life worth “imitating”? Which part would you least like others to see?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zhiyuan, after pressing send, how would you begin that first lunch?
lessons.jesus: At a well, Jesus met a Samaritan woman and opened the conversation with three words: “Give me a drink” (John 4:7). He began with one person and one conversation, and in the end “from that city many of the Samaritans believed in him” (John 4:39). He never thinks one person is too few, because each one is someone he was willing to die to find.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for finding me through one person, one meal, one conversation. Show me today the person you want me to walk with. Give me courage to send that invitation and patience to hear their story first. Let me bring them not to myself but to you, and may the one I walk with one day walk with others too. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: After praying, write down the name of someone to walk with
Invite them for coffee or lunch today
Prepare one true story of God at work in your job
lessons.noon: “commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” — Lord, right now I am willing to pass on what you have given me to the one beside me.

mem.t: If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

lessons.title: Two by Two into the Fire
lessons.theme: Kingdom work is never a solo mission; a team of co-workers begins “two by two”

v: He called to himself the twelve, and began to send them out two by two; and he gave them authority over the unclean spirits.
Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he was about to come.
Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the labourers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out labourers into his harvest.

lessons.still: Bring your palms together lightly, like two people high-fiving before they set out. Say: “Lord, you never send people out one by one. Today I won’t play the hero; show me the co-worker you are sending out with me.”
teach: Twice Jesus sent out his disciples, and both times he used the same method. He “called to himself the twelve, and began to send them out two by two; and he gave them authority”. Later he appointed seventy others and “sent them two by two ahead of him”. He could have sent seventy teams to cover more towns; instead he sent thirty-five. In Jesus’ arithmetic, partnership matters more than efficiency. And he said, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the labourers are few” — the work is vast, which is exactly why no one should do it alone.

Fire services have an iron rule: no one enters a burning building alone. Always in pairs. In thick smoke you lose your bearings, and if one person collapses, no one knows. Two go in: one handles the hose, the other searches; each watches the other’s air gauge, ready to drag their partner out. Work can feel like a fire with no visible exit: redundancies, mergers, office politics. God doesn’t want you charging in alone. He gives you a partner, to go in together and come out together.

Last week we learnt to find a spiritual companion. This week we take a step further: from companion to team. A team doesn’t begin when ten people sign up; it begins when two receive a commission together. The self-centred life wants to be a lone ranger, keeping the rewards and the credit. The self-emptied life gladly works in partnership, because the work is the Lord’s, not mine. So don’t rush to run a big event at the company. First ask, “Lord, whom are you sending out with me?” Then together pray the Lord of the harvest to send out more labourers.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 235 begins with the “2” and moves towards the “5”, a team of comrades. People matter more than tasks: Jesus would rather reach fewer towns than send his disciples out alone. Building God’s order starts with two people sent out together.
lessons.scene: Haoran is a sales rep at a pharmaceutical company in Guangzhou. Several Christians work there, scattered across departments. He wants to start a lunchtime Bible study and has already designed the poster, planning to organise it all himself. Then he remembers Yuxuan in finance — also a Christian, careful and thorough, though they barely know each other. Holding the printed poster, Haoran stands outside the finance office, hesitating to knock.
q: Who is God? — Jesus would rather send fewer teams than send anyone out alone. What does that show you about how he values co-workers?
Who am I? — In ministry or at work, are you more of a lone ranger, or willing to partner with someone?
How shall I respond? — If you were Haoran, after knocking, how would you invite Yuxuan to co-lead the Bible study?
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself never worked alone. He said, “He who sent me is with me. The Father hasn’t left me alone” (John 8:29). The Son works with the Father and sends the Spirit to be with us. When he sent his disciples out two by two, he brought the pattern of the triune God’s partnership into human life; and when he sends us, he never lets us go alone.
lessons.pray: Lord of the harvest, thank you for sending me, and for not sending me alone. I confess I often want to get everything done by myself, thinking partnership is too much trouble. Forgive the lone ranger in me, and show me the co-worker you have prepared. Together we ask you: in my company and my industry, send out more labourers into your harvest. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one piece of service you have meant to do alone
Pray about it and ask the Lord to show you a co-worker
Invite that person to pray or have lunch with you today
lessons.noon: “began to send them out two by two” — Lord, right now I won’t go it alone; I set out with the co-worker you have given me.

lessons.title: The Lazy Susan
lessons.theme: A team of one accord is bound together by teaching, fellowship, bread and prayer

v: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.
All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favour with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.

lessons.still: Pick up your breakfast or coffee and pause before you eat. Think of the colleagues you will see today and say for each one, “Lord, bless them.” Then say: “Lord, let my table today be a place of your presence too.”
teach: After Pentecost the life of the early church stood on four pillars: “They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.” Truth, fellowship, table, prayer — none can be missing. They “had all things in common”, sharing “according as anyone had need”. Day by day they were together in the temple and ate at home “with gladness and singleness of heart”. The result? They had “favour with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.”

At a Chinese banquet, the cleverest thing is the lazy Susan in the middle of the round table. Each dish goes on, the turntable spins, and everyone can reach it. There is no gap between the head of the table and the foot; whoever needs it, it turns towards them. The unity of the early church was like that turntable: not everyone the same, but good things moving round the middle. A team at work can be the same — information not hoarded, credit not grabbed, hardship carried together, resources turned towards the colleague who needs them most.

Notice the order: first the word of God and prayer, then the generosity of shared possessions. Unity is not manufactured by team-building days or slogans; it is the fruit of the Spirit working in each heart. A self-centred team calculates privately — cooperating in public, comparing in secret. A self-emptied team lives for Jesus, for others, not for itself, and joy and attractiveness follow naturally. A changed life changes daily living, and changed daily living changes relationships.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationship, then ministry. The unity of the early church began in the word and prayer, flowed out to tables and wallets, and ended with “The Lord added … day by day.” God’s order is something that flows out of life.
lessons.scene: Xinmin runs a twenty-person renovation company in Johor Bahru, with Chinese, Malay and Indonesian workers. Last week the son of Ah Feng, one of his foremen, was admitted to hospital, and the medical bills are crushing him; everyone on site knows. At lunch today, standing by the site cabin, Xinmin wonders whether to suggest a voluntary mutual-help fund — and fears it will look like a boss putting on a show.
q: Who is God? — In “The Lord added to the assembly day by day”, what do you see about how God uses a community of one accord?
Who am I? — On your team, do you tend to hoard resources or let good things move around?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xinmin, how would you raise the idea so that it is love, not a show?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper the disciples argued about who was greatest, and Jesus said, “I am amongst you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). He was the host, yet he served at the table himself. The early church could share everything with one accord because they had first been served and changed by this self-giving Lord. He is the true host of that table.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you are among us as one who serves. Let my team be not just people who work together, but a community that cares for one another. On building sites, in offices and kitchens, keep us from hoarding, from competing for credit and from coldness; let us share each other’s loads when needs arise. May people see us and see your love. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Invite a colleague who usually eats alone to join you for lunch
Share a useful resource with your team without being asked
Notice a colleague’s struggle and do one small thing to help
lessons.noon: “they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart” — Lord, right now let my lunch break, too, be full of your presence and joy.

lessons.title: Tents and a Church
lessons.theme: Priscilla and Aquila served together in their trade, opened their home and built others up in love

v: After these things Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth.

He found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He came to them,
and because he practised the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers.
Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures.
This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

lessons.still: Picture your front door, your shop door, your office door. Say quietly: “Lord, every space I have is yours. If someone today needs welcome or building up, open my door for you.”
teach: Aquila and Priscilla were a Jewish couple expelled from Rome, and “by trade they were tent makers”. When Paul came to Corinth, “because he practised the same trade, he lived with them and worked.” They stitched tents together and served together. Later they met the eloquent Apollos and found he “knew only the baptism of John”, so “they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.” Paul calls them “my fellow workers in Christ Jesus”, with a church meeting in their house (Romans 16:3–5).

In old Asian market streets you find the shophouse: the shop at the front for trade and customers, the home behind or above for cooking, rest and welcoming friends. Priscilla and Aquila lived in that kind of layout. At the front: stitching tents, keeping accounts, delivering orders. Behind: an open home, Bible study, companionship with fellow workers. They did not split work and ministry into two halves; under one roof there was both honest business and a warm church.

Most moving is how they treated Apollos. They did not correct him publicly in the synagogue and embarrass him; they took him aside — privately, thoroughly, lovingly. People matter more than tasks, and relationship matters more than winning the argument. The self-emptied life doesn’t need to prove it knows more; it only wants to help others know the Lord better. Apollos went on to become a powerful fellow worker. Couples who work together, business partners and colleagues can all become a “church in the tent” like this.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Never hurt people for the sake of a task. By taking Apollos aside and explaining more accurately, Priscilla and Aquila protected both truth and relationship. Humility draws out humility; building up one person is building God’s order.
lessons.scene: Ziying and her husband run a brunch café in Kaohsiung. Ah Zhe, a part-time barista who recently came to faith, is on fire, and keeps telling customers, “Believe in Jesus and you’ll get rich and never get ill!” Today he said it to a regular who has just lost his job, and the man’s face fell. Behind the counter, coffee pot in hand, Ziying wants to correct him on the spot — then remembers she could ask him to stay for dinner after closing.
q: Who is God? — God used a tent-making couple to build up Apollos. What does that show you about how he values ordinary work and homes?
Who am I? — When a colleague or team member gets something wrong, do you usually correct them publicly, or take them aside?
How shall I respond? — If you were Ziying, how would you help Ah Zhe understand the gospel more accurately?
lessons.jesus: After Peter denied him three times, the risen Jesus did not call him to account in front of everyone. He lit a charcoal fire by the lake and said, “Come and eat breakfast!” (John 21:12). Only after the meal did he gently ask, “Do you love me?” He restored a relationship and renewed a calling over breakfast. Priscilla’s table is a shadow of this Lord.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that when I fell, you did not shame me in public but prepared breakfast for me. Let my shop, my office and my home be places where you welcome people. When I see a colleague’s mistake, give me a gentle heart and the right moment to help them privately and thoroughly, so that they know you better — not so that I look more spiritual. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray first for someone who needs gentle correction
Invite them for a private meal or tea instead of correcting publicly
Open your home or office this week to welcome a colleague
lessons.noon: “they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately” — Lord, right now let me treat people with love and patience, not just with right and wrong.

lessons.title: Coals Burn Together
lessons.theme: A workplace group need not be large; where two or three gather in his name, the Lord is there

v: Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.”
Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works,
not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.

lessons.still: Count three slow breaths. Say: “Lord, you said that where two or three gather in your name, you are there. Today I don’t ask for numbers, only for your presence.” Then think of someone you could pray with today.
teach: Jesus set the threshold remarkably low: “where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.” Not two or three hundred, not a stage, a band and a venue — just two or three, in his name. He also promised: “if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.” Hebrews adds: don’t forsake “our own assembling together”, but “consider how to provoke one another to love and good works”.

Anyone who has done a barbecue knows that coals burn best together. Push one glowing coal off to the side and before long it dims and goes cold; put it back in the pile and it glows again. Christians at work are like that coal. Lit up on Sunday, then on Monday nudged aside by meetings, targets and office gossip, they slowly cool. A workplace group of two or three puts the coals back together.

You don’t need permission for a meeting room or a large enough number to begin a workplace group. It can be twenty minutes at lunch, a video call after work, or five minutes before a shift change in the factory. The format is not the point; “in my name” is — letting Jesus be King, not letting complaints or gossip be king. With eyes on Jesus, the group has fire; with eyes on people, it becomes just another pantry chat.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 235 begins with the “2”. Two or three gathered in the Lord’s name are the smallest unit of God’s order. Lean on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head: the presence he promises matters more than any programme we plan.
lessons.scene: Caleb is a software engineer at a fully remote company in Wellington. The only other Christian he knows of is Esther, a colleague in Sydney. After this morning’s stand-up he opens the company chat to message her: “Twenty-minute video prayer on Thursday lunch breaks?” He worries it might look like preaching on company time.
q: Who is God? — Jesus promises to be among two or three. What does that show you about how he values small gatherings?
Who am I? — From Monday to Friday, are your spiritual coals kept together, or pushed aside to cool?
How shall I respond? — If you were Caleb, how would you invite Esther while respecting the company’s time and policies?
lessons.jesus: On the evening of the resurrection, the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, “for fear of the Jews”. “Jesus came and stood in the middle and said to them, ‘Peace be to you.’” (John 20:19). He did not wait until they were braver or more numerous. Locked doors could not keep him out, and neither can a screen; wherever two or three are, he is there.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that you do not despise small numbers. I confess that after Monday my heart often slowly cools. Give me two or three companions to gather in your name — at lunch, before a shift, on a video call. Stand among us and give us your peace, and let us provoke one another to love and good works. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Choose a regular weekly time that doesn’t use working hours
Invite one or two Christian colleagues to pray together
Pray for your company and your manager for three minutes today
lessons.noon: “where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them” — Lord, right now I believe you are here.

lessons.title: A Soft Opening for the Group
lessons.theme: Write a plan for a workplace overcomers’ group in faith, and rise up and build

v: Then I said to them, “You see the bad situation that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste, and its gates are burnt with fire. Come, let’s build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we won’t be disgraced.”

I told them about the hand of my God which was good on me, and also about the king’s words that he had spoken to me. They said, “Let’s rise up and build.” So they strengthened their hands for the good work.

lessons.still: Take out a sheet of paper or open your notes app, but don’t write yet. Say: “Lord, this is your work, not my plan. Let your good hand help me, so that every line I write comes from you.”
teach: When Nehemiah saw the ruined walls of Jerusalem, he first fasted and prayed, then inspected the walls, and only then gathered the people: “Come, let’s build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we won’t be disgraced.” He didn’t just share an ideal; he testified about “the hand of my God which was good on me”. The people answered, “Let’s rise up and build.” So “they strengthened their hands for the good work.” Vision, prayer, plan and unity — none can be missing.

Before a new restaurant officially opens, it often has a soft opening: limited hours, part of the menu, friends and family only, adjusting as it goes. A workplace overcomers’ group can start the same way. You don’t need a grand vision statement or a constitution. Try a four-to-six-week soft opening: two or three people, a fixed time, a simple pattern — read a passage, share one thing from work, pray for each other, each take one small action. Afterwards, review, correct, and carry on.

As you write your plan, ask five questions. Who? (which two or three names to pray for) When? (which slot each week) Where? (a meeting room, a canteen, online) What? (Scripture, sharing, prayer, action) Why? (so that Jesus is King in my workplace). This is not a KPI for yourself but a response to God. Of the eight steps, practice, review, correction and repetition all happen in this small soft opening.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Practice, review, correction and repetition from the eight steps. A plan is not head-driven bravado but a heart response to the Spirit. Starting with two or three is building God’s order in the workplace.
lessons.scene: Jia Hao is a night-shift supervisor at a semiconductor plant in Penang, responsible for forty operators. On his 3 a.m. break in the staff canteen, he types into his phone: “Overcomers’ group soft opening: Tuesdays, 15 minutes before shift change.” Below are two blank lines for names. He thinks of two colleagues — one recently baptised, one whose marriage is in trouble — and his finger stops on the screen.
q: Who is God? — In “the hand of my God which was good on me”, what do you see about how God takes part in our plans?
Who am I? — When it comes to starting a group, do you tend to get stuck on lack of vision, lack of a plan, or lack of courage?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jia Hao, how would you pray over those two blank lines, and how would you invite them?
lessons.jesus: Before choosing the twelve apostles, Jesus “went out to the mountain to pray, and he continued all night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12). Only at daybreak did he call his disciples and choose from among them. The Son of God built his team beginning with prayer. His plan was not a slide deck but the will he received before the Father; our group plans must grow out of prayer too.
lessons.pray: Gracious God, thank you for placing me in this workplace. I put my group plan into your hands: show me the two or three names, prepare their hearts, and give me courage to invite them. Let us start small and adjust as we go, not seeking to perform but only for you to be King among us, so that this group becomes a lamp in the company. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write your group plan: who, when, where, what
Pray for every name on the plan
Send one of them a soft-opening invitation today
lessons.noon: “Let’s rise up and build” — Lord, right now I rise up in faith to build together with you.

mem.t: Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

lessons.title: Your Kingdom Come
lessons.theme: God’s Kingdom truly comes to the workplace wherever I obey his will

v: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
who delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love,

lessons.still: Plant both feet on the floor and feel the ground beneath you. Pray slowly: “Our Father in heaven, may your Kingdom come to this office, this desk, the very spot where my feet stand. Today, let your will be done in me.”
teach: The first three requests of the Lord’s Prayer are all about God: your name, your Kingdom, your will. “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” God’s Kingdom is not only a future heaven; it is wherever God reigns. Paul says God “delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love”. We are already citizens of that Kingdom. Every day we go to work carrying heavenly citizenship into an earthly workplace.

A chain’s head office sets service standards, but the real test is not the presentation at headquarters; it is every branch. Does the cashier follow them? Does the night-shift worker keep them? “As it is in heaven” means letting the standards of heaven’s head office be lived out in every branch on earth. Your desk, your building site, your ward, your kitchen is a branch of God’s Kingdom, and the decisions you make determine whether that branch looks like head office.

To pray “Your Kingdom come” is also to pray “my kingdom go”. The self-centred life goes to work to expand its own kingdom: my results, my territory, my reputation. Letting Jesus be King means handing him the final say over every choice. It is a shift of perspective — from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal. God’s Kingdom does not advance by slogans. It comes quietly in the moment someone says, “not what I desire”.
lessons.light: 321 Light: One of the two cores is to let Jesus be King. God’s Kingdom comes to the workplace not first by changing systems, but by letting Jesus be King in my heart. Changed thinking changes life, and changed life changes how we live.
lessons.scene: Jiawei is a wealth adviser at a bank in Taipei, well short of his quarterly target. This afternoon seventy-eight-year-old Uncle Chen comes in about a maturing fixed deposit, and Jiawei’s manager hints that he should push a high-commission, high-risk structured product. Jiawei looks at the old man’s trusting eyes, and at the product leaflet in his hand, open at the risk disclosure page.
q: Who is God? — Praying “Our Father in heaven”, what relationship do you see between you and this reigning God?
Who am I? — At work, are you more often expanding “my kingdom” or letting “God’s Kingdom” come?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jiawei, what would God’s will being “done on earth” look like at this moment?
lessons.jesus: Jesus taught his disciples to pray, “Let your will be done on earth”, and in Gethsemane he prayed it first himself: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). He obeyed all the way to the cross, and through his death and resurrection God’s Kingdom came to us. He did not only teach us the prayer; he lived it for us first.
lessons.pray: Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy and may your Kingdom come in my work. When targets push me to compromise, when a manager wants me to say what isn’t true, give me courage to say, “not what I desire, but what you desire.” Let every client I serve see in me the justice and mercy of your Kingdom. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly before work
Before one decision today, ask: “Is this God’s will?”
Be honest about the limits of a product or service
lessons.noon: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” — Lord, right now reign at my desk.

lessons.title: The Power of a Mustard Seed
lessons.theme: God’s Kingdom begins with small, unnoticed things, yet can change a whole workplace

v: He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed which a man took, and sowed in his field,
which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches.”
He spoke another parable to them. “The Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until it was all leavened.”

lessons.still: Hold out your palm and imagine a seed smaller than a sesame seed resting in it. Say: “Lord, what I can do today may be very small, but I give this little bit to you. Let it grow in your hands.”
teach: Jesus describes the Kingdom in two parables. “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed”, smaller than all seeds, yet it grows until it “becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches”. And “the Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until it was all leavened.” The mustard seed speaks of outward growth, from small to great; the yeast speaks of inward permeation, from within to without. God’s Kingdom never starts with fanfare. It starts small and hidden.

In a spreadsheet, get the formula right in the first cell, drag it down, and the whole column of hundreds of rows calculates correctly. Get the first cell wrong, and the whole column is wrong too. One small choice of yours at work — delivering on time, remembering the cleaner’s name, speaking up for a colleague who is being ignored in a meeting — looks like a single cell, yet it can be “dragged down” and change the culture of an entire department.

The self-centred life despises small things, because they aren’t visible or noticed enough. The self-emptied life is glad to be the seed that falls into the ground, the yeast that is hidden. We don’t need to become the most powerful person in the company to shape its culture. We only need to be faithful where we are, letting the life of Christ seep out little by little. Growth belongs to God: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6).
lessons.light: 321 Light: The five-fold change from within: thinking, life, living, relationships, ministry. Yeast works from the inside, and God’s Kingdom first changes what is inside me, then the people around me, then the whole workplace.
lessons.scene: Zhenhao is HR manager at an electronics factory in Shenzhen with three thousand workers. He has noticed that the hot water in the dormitories often fails, and that many new hires quit within three months. He wants to start with two small things: fix the water heaters, and have an experienced worker eat with each newcomer during their first week. The owner sneers: “A factory this size — what difference will that make?” Zhenhao stands at the office door, unsure how to answer.
q: Who is God? — Through the mustard seed and the yeast, what do you see about how God uses tiny things to do great things?
Who am I? — Have you ever given up doing the right thing because “it’s too small to matter”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zhenhao, how would you answer the owner, and how would you keep doing those two small things?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). He himself is that seed: born in a manger, raised in a small town, dying on a cross, buried in a tomb. What looked like the smallest, most defeated moment bore fruit that has filled the earth.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for beginning the rescue of the world in the smallest place. Forgive me for so often despising small things, wanting only to do big things and be noticed. Today, let me live out your Kingdom faithfully in one cell of a spreadsheet, one greeting, one tank of hot water. I give this tiny seed to you; please make it grow. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Learn the name of a frontline colleague and use it
Make one small process easier for your colleagues
Pray for one minute for the culture of your department
lessons.noon: “The Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast” — Lord, right now let your life quietly spread from within me to those around me.

lessons.title: A Granary in the Famine
lessons.theme: One faithful person can bring blessing to a whole organisation and society

v: The seven years of plenty, that were in the land of Egypt, came to an end.
The seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
When all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do.”
The famine was over all the surface of the earth. Joseph opened all the store houses, and sold to the Egyptians. The famine was severe in the land of Egypt.
All countries came into Egypt, to Joseph, to buy grain, because the famine was severe in all the earth.

From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. The LORD’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field.

lessons.still: Picture a well-ordered granary, sacks of grain neatly stacked. Say: “Lord, everything I manage today — time, budget, data, people — is entrusted by you. Let me look after it faithfully and become a blessing to others when they are in need.”
teach: When Joseph was a slave in Potiphar’s house, “the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake.” Later, as governor, he stored grain through seven years of plenty. When famine came, “There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.” Pharaoh told the people, “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do.” In the end, “All countries came into Egypt, to Joseph.” One God-fearing man brought blessing to a household, a nation and even the whole earth.

Anyone in purchasing or warehousing knows about safety stock. In good times you hold a little extra of the critical parts, so that if the supply chain breaks, the production line can keep going. Joseph built safety stock in the years of plenty. He didn’t squander the good years, nor did he price-gouge in the bad ones; he opened the storehouses and sold grain so people could live. At work, honest accounts, forward planning and fairness to people are all granaries prepared for a famine.

Joseph later told his brothers, “God meant it for good, to save many people alive” (Genesis 50:20). His authority was used not for revenge but for preservation; his wisdom was not for himself but for everyone. This is self-emptied leadership: self-denial means living for Jesus, for others, not for myself. When we are faithful in our position and just in the face of profit, a company or a community may be blessed because of us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: One purpose — to build God’s order. Joseph built a granary system in the fear of God, so that God received glory and the nations received bread. A shift of perspective: from temporary gain to eternal blessing.
lessons.scene: Yalan is purchasing manager at a food wholesaler in Kuala Lumpur. Days of heavy rain have brought floods and shortages, and competitors have tripled the price of cooking oil. The extra stock she ordered three months ago is sitting in the warehouse. In the meeting, the boss says: “Here’s our chance — raise prices with everyone else!” Yalan looks at the list of small restaurant customers she knows so well, and raises her hand.
q: Who is God? — God blessed Egypt for Joseph’s sake. What does that show you about how he blesses many through one?
Who am I? — In your work, are you more like someone who squanders the years of plenty, or someone who prepares a granary?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yalan, having raised your hand, what would you propose to your boss?
lessons.jesus: Joseph was sold by his brothers, yet became the one who fed them. Jesus was rejected by his own, yet became bread for the whole world. He said, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry” (John 6:35). Joseph opened Egypt’s storehouses; Jesus allowed his own body to be broken, so that in our spiritual famine we might be filled.
lessons.pray: Lord who provides bread, thank you for feeding me with yourself when I was empty. Keep me from squandering in years of plenty and from greed in years of famine; when I could earn more, help me remember justice and mercy. Let my company and my department be blessed through my faithfulness, and let people see in me that you are the bread of life. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Check one resource you manage and prepare it well
When setting a price or allocating today, think of the weaker party first
Pray for someone at work who is going through hardship
lessons.noon: “in all the land of Egypt there was bread” — Lord, right now let me be a blessing to those around me in their famine.

lessons.title: Foundations, Steel and Wiring
lessons.theme: A godly culture is built on God-fearing values, sound systems and healthy relationships

v: Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

Let them judge the people at all times. It shall be that every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves. So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you.
If you will do this thing, and God commands you so, then you will be able to endure, and all these people also will go to their place in peace.”
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

lessons.still: Sit up straight and take three deep breaths, like a building standing firm on its foundations. Say: “Lord, be the foundation of my life and my work. Let everything I build today be built on you.”
teach: Moses judged the people from morning till evening, and his father-in-law Jethro said, “The thing that you do is not good” (Exodus 18:17). He advised Moses to choose “able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain”, as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. They would judge small matters and bring great ones to Moses. The outcome: “you will be able to endure, and all these people also will go to their place in peace.” The prophet Micah names the core values: “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God”.

When you put up a building, what you see is the façade; what you don’t see, yet matters most, is three things: foundations, steel frame and wiring. A godly workplace culture is the same. The foundations are values — fear of God, honesty, justice, mercy. The steel frame is systems — clear roles, sensible delegation, fair processes. The wiring is relationships — trust, honest conversation, shared hardship. Fine slogans without foundations crack at the first tremor; systems without relationships are like a building with no power — cold and unliveable.

Jethro’s advice is more than a management technique; it is spiritual humility. Moses admitted he was not all-sufficient and was willing to let go, so that others could “share the load”. The self-centred leader has to approve everything, unable to trust and unwilling to release power. The self-emptied leader lets people be people and God be God, developing and trusting others. People matter more than tasks: systems exist to protect people, not to drain them. A culture built like this is God’s order.
lessons.light: 321 Light: One purpose — to build God’s order. Values, systems and relationships must all centre on God. Humility means laying down power and returning to my place; only by delegating can others “share the load”, so that everyone goes home in peace.
lessons.scene: Zijian runs a twenty-two-person landscape design firm in Christchurch, and every quote, drawing and client email goes through him. This month two senior designers handed in their notice, saying, “We can’t make any decisions here.” Tonight he sits in the empty office with two resignation letters and a blank sheet of paper, wondering whether to write down the company’s values first or try to keep his staff.
q: Who is God? — “God commands you so”: what does that show you about how God cares for systems at work and people’s peace?
Who am I? — On your team, which most needs repair: foundations, steel frame or wiring?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zijian, what would you write first on that blank sheet tonight?
lessons.jesus: When the disciples argued about greatness, Jesus said, “whoever desires to become great amongst you shall be your servant”, “even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve” (Matthew 20:26–28). He overturned the world’s culture of power and built a Kingdom with service at its heart. A godly culture is the pattern of Jesus becoming a team’s everyday life.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for being the foundation of my life. I confess I often want to control everything and find it hard to trust others. Give me Jethro’s wisdom and Moses’ teachable heart. Help me build values that fear you, fair systems and real relationships in my team, so that my colleagues can work here in peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down three values you want your team to hold
Delegate one decision to a suitable colleague
Ask one colleague today how they really feel about their work
lessons.noon: “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” — Lord, right now let me walk with you in my work.

lessons.title: My Kingdom Blueprint at Work
lessons.theme: Write down plainly the vision God puts in your heart, and seek the peace of where you are

v: The LORD answered me, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.
For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries towards the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it, because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.”

lessons.still: Close your eyes and imagine your workplace a year from now. Don’t think about results first; think about people. Say: “Lord, what is your heart for this place? Let me see it, and let me have a part in it.”
teach: God told Habakkuk, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.” A vision should be written down, clear enough to read on the run; and “Though it takes time, wait for it, because it will surely come.” Jeremiah wrote to the exiles in Babylon, not telling them to hide and wait to go home, but saying: “Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.” Even a foreign city was a place God wanted them to bless.

Many companies write OKRs each year: one objective, three key results. A Kingdom blueprint can be written the same way, with a different objective. Not “I get promoted”, but “Jesus is King here”. The key results can follow the five-fold change: What needs to change in my thinking? What fruit should grow in my life? What work habits need adjusting? Which one or two people will I walk with? With whom will I serve? Put it on one page, and pin it where you can see it.

A Kingdom blueprint is not a scorecard for hitting targets; it is a response to God. We write it down to remember, to pray, and to review with our companions. Success is not proof, and failure is not condemnation; even if progress is slow, “wait for it”, because it is God who completes the work. The eight steps begin with information, revelation and conviction; today they arrive at practice — turning God’s vision into something you can do at work tomorrow.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The five-fold change from within — thinking, life, living, relationships, ministry. Write your Kingdom blueprint along these five layers, with your eyes on Jesus rather than your own performance, so that Jesus receives all the glory.
lessons.scene: Huimin is head nurse on a ward at a hospital in Tainan, leading thirty nurses across three shifts. Staff shortages and a wave of resignations have left the ward demoralised. After handover today she stands at the whiteboard in the nurses’ station, marker in hand, wanting to write in the corner: “May this ward be a place of healing and hope.” She worries her colleagues will think her naïve.
q: Who is God? — God told the exiles to “seek the peace of the city”. What does that show you about his heart for your workplace?
Who am I? — Of thinking, life, living, relationships and ministry, where do you most want God to renew you?
How shall I respond? — If you were Huimin, beyond writing on the whiteboard, what could the first step of your Kingdom blueprint be?
lessons.jesus: In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus declared his mission: “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18). He knew exactly what the Father had sent him to do, and at the end could say, “I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4). Those who follow him receive his mission and carry it into their own workplaces.
lessons.pray: God who gives vision, thank you for your good purposes for my workplace. Put your vision in my heart; help me write it plainly and live it faithfully. I seek the peace of my company, my department and my colleagues. When progress is slow and no one sees results, help me keep waiting, trusting that you will complete it. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write your workplace Kingdom blueprint on one page
Share one goal from your blueprint with your companion
Pray today for the peace of your company or unit
lessons.noon: “Seek the peace of the city” — Lord, right now I seek the peace of my workplace and every colleague in it.

mem.t: He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne.

lessons.title: I Have Fought the Good Fight
lessons.theme: Overcoming is not winning one battle but finishing the whole course faithfully

v: For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure has come.
I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.
From now on, the crown of righteousness is stored up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing.

lessons.still: Imagine today is your last day in this job. Be still for thirty seconds and say: “Lord, if today were the finish line, I want you to find me faithful. Every small task today, I do for you.”
teach: When Paul wrote this letter he was in a Roman prison, knowing martyrdom was near. “For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure has come.” Then come three sentences that sum up his life: “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.” He doesn’t say, “I won every battle,” or list the churches he planted. He says: I fought it, I finished it, I kept it. Ahead lies “the crown of righteousness”, given not to him only, “but also to all those who have loved his appearing”.

On someone’s last day before leaving or retiring, they clear their desk: hand back the access card, tidy the files for whoever takes over, wipe the desk clean, say goodbye to colleagues one by one. In that moment what matters most is rarely your job title. It is this: am I leaving a mess, or a clear handover? Between me and my colleagues, is there debt or blessing? Paul’s “departure” is like a faithful employee clearing his desk: what needed handing over has been handed over, what needed keeping has been kept, and he can go to meet the Lord in peace.

This is the last week of our fifty-two-week journey. An overcomer is not someone who never falls, but someone who falls, rises again by grace, and keeps running. The self-centred life prizes the excitement of the start; the self-emptied life prizes faithfulness at the finish. A shift of perspective: from a temporary appraisal to an eternal crown. Your work may never appear in the company history, but “the Lord, the righteous judge” has seen it all, and he is keeping a crown for you with his own hands.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The goal is to become an overcomer. Eyes on Jesus, not on my own record: success is not proof, failure is not condemnation. Faithfully finishing the course set before me is letting Jesus receive all the glory.
lessons.scene: Liren has served at a district office in Taipei for thirty-four years and retires tomorrow. At this afternoon’s farewell tea, the section chief asks him to say a few words. He holds a prepared speech listing every portfolio he handled and every award he received. Looking at the young colleagues in front of him, he turns the page over, wondering whether to say something different.
q: Who is God? — “The Lord, the righteous judge” keeps a crown for the faithful. What kind of Lord do you see?
Who am I? — If today were your last day in this job, how would you want colleagues to remember you?
How shall I respond? — If you were Liren, what would you write on the back of that page?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus said, “It is finished!” (John 19:30). He did not give up halfway; he completed the work of redemption the Father had given him. “For the joy that was set before him” he “endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2). We can finish the course because he finished it first for us, and runs every step beside us.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for running the road to the cross for me and saying, “It is finished.” Looking back on this year, I see faithfulness and I see weakness; cover it all with your grace. In every job and every handover, let me leave clear accounts and warm relationships, until on that day I can say before you: I have finished the course. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Tidy one work document so the next person can follow it
